This is a preface or introduction page from a manuscript of the 'Aja'ib al-makhluqat (Wonders of Creation), written in Ottoman Turkish. The text reads approximately as follows:

A letter to a great and noble merchant, and to a man of high standing among the elect. This mine of benefits and subjects is the book of wonders and marvels, sent quickly by Abu al-Fadl. Every science that the people seek is contained within it — indeed, it encompasses all knowledge. By his command, a noble scholar began the Mathnawi [verse exposition] of this book, setting out its arrangement, adding nothing beyond what is proper. Rather, he set forth clear mention and sound reflection, so that the realities therein might be understood, and the wisdom of the Maker become fully manifest, and the rational person be left without excuse. And this is why the Messenger of God, upon him be peace and blessings, used to say: 'I seek refuge in God from all things' — that for whatever one reflects upon among the works of creation, one's certainty, faith, conviction, and acknowledgment increase, and the spiritual taste grows. Hence the Prophet, God bless him and grant him peace, said: 'Reflect upon the creation of God' — and this is the deepest understanding. He completed it, making it a source of goodness for the learned and the worthy, refining the soul and purifying it; thereafter one's insight becomes like pure water. Among the most wondrous things mentioned is the story of Khidr and Moses, upon them both be peace — and here begins the story of Moses, upon him be peace.

A divine revelation came down, saying: Go to such-and-such a place, in a certain manner, and from there proceed to perform the dawn prayer. Moses, peace be upon him, did as commanded. By chance, a horseman came along and took a purse from beside that spring, then departed. Afterward came another man searching for the purse; he found it there, took it, and left. Then, later, came yet another, bearing a bundle on his back. He too came along that road, and that man himself also passed. He came out of the water nearby, rested for a moment for relief, sat down, let his horse drink, then used the purse. He came and asked: 'Has anyone found my purse?' The first man arose in anger, struck him, and killed him. Moses, peace be upon him, witnessed all these events and supplicated to the presence of the Divine Truth, saying: 'O Lord! Where is the justice in all of this, in the presence of the Divine Truth?' Revelation came: 'That first horseman's father had been killed by this second man's father, and retribution had not been carried out. The amount of gold that was in the first horseman's bag equaled precisely what the second man's father owed to the first man's father. Thus I arranged in this world that each person received what was rightfully owed to them — and I am the Judge with Justice.' From this it becomes clear that the inner mysteries cannot be comprehended by just anyone's sight and perception. The author of this book, hearing and seeing, following the path of reflection and contemplation, wished to record these rare and wonderful things — which had not been compiled elsewhere — together in a book, for the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, has said: 'Bind knowledge by writing it down.' Thus, what is written becomes established even if there is error, and it benefits others; and it relieves the burden of those who study it.

And know that the mind's imagination and its rejection of something does not arise from the intelligence of one who has never denied anything, for God Almighty has great power over what is possible, to bring it into existence as He wills. And the things mentioned in the books of wonders of the creation of God Almighty are of two kinds: some are perceptible to the senses, and some are known through rational proof. And one marvels at hearing them, or they are written accounts of strange properties known through experience. For example, a person may experience that a certain thing prolongs life indefinitely, yet if in some cases the experience proves otherwise, it is not permissible to reject all such things on account of a failure in some cases. For 'There is no sense in abandoning all matters on account of failure in some of them.' For sometimes the failure occurs because a condition was not met, or because an obstacle arose — just as you would reckon with a magnet and iron: if the magnet is brought close to iron and the iron does not respond, one should not say the property of the magnet is nullified, for when vinegar is removed from those things, the property is restored. And if you see a magnet, do not say iron cannot be attracted — rather, there is something preventing it that is not known. Therefore it is necessary to begin with a preliminary introduction so that the purpose of the book may be understood. These are the introductions I have begun. THE FIRST INTRODUCTION: ON THE EXPLANATION OF WONDER. It is strange that a person is struck with wonder at something of which one has little knowledge — as when one does not know the manner of its action. For example, if a man sees a beehive and watches the bees building it, he may say in amazement: 'How extraordinary is this arrangement!' And even if it seems to him that the bees arranged this by instinct, he would be seized with astonishment that a creature of this kind builds these honeycombs whose sides are all equal — such that a complete and perfect engineer could scarcely achieve the like.

And from the honey that has been collected and divided into portions, distributed from house to house — it is not contrary to the established custom. It was gathered according to one recipe and stored, and a supply was laid up for winter, for in winter food is scarce in the desert. It is necessary to store provisions, and these stores are kept in vessels, covered with lids and sealed with wax and resin so that the honey is not spoiled by dust, wind, or other things, and it remains preserved within. 

How wondrous: the person who comes into this world and from the very beginning of his morning sees these marvels — until his reason matures and he is occupied with his livelihood and pursues worldly pleasures — becomes so accustomed to them that when he looks more carefully, he is astonished. If he encounters anything contrary to the normal course of things, he finds it remarkable and exclaims 'Glory be to God, there is no god but God.' Yet throughout his entire life, these things have been before him, and the intellects of wise men and the minds of the discerning are bewildered by them. If you can picture this meaning: look up at the celestial spheres — bodies so refined and yet of such vast extent — consider how God the Most High preserves them from change and corruption throughout the age of the world, holding all the heavenly orbs together like a single ring in the desert. God Most High has said: 'And the sky — We built it with might, and indeed We are its expanders.' 

Then look at how the different celestial revolutions vary: some are slow relative to others, some are fluid, some are obstructing, and some move swiftly while others move slowly. Then look at how they move continuously, never resting or pausing for even a single moment. Then look at how each one follows the other without connection or attachment. And then look at the stars —

The position of the sun and the moon, and the variation of their rising and setting points, is the cause of the differences in seasons, which in turn give rise to animals and plants. After this, consider how the reckoning set down neither falls short nor exceeds. Then consider the number of the celestial bodies and their multitude, and the variation among them: some incline toward red, some toward a darker hue, and some retain their original color. After this, consider the course of the sun in its sphere, for it completes one full revolution around a locality, rising one day and setting, alternating between night and day — times of activity and times of rest — and between night and day there are short and long periods. The seasons of the year arise from the mean distance of the sun, and thus every land obtains its four seasons. The scholars of natural philosophy are in agreement that the body of the sun is vastly greater than the globe of the earth, and the greatest sphere encompasses the entire world. Despite this, its speed of motion is immense — and proof of this statement is the following:

Anecdote — The Messenger of God, may God's peace and blessings be upon him, when the time of the midday prayer was approaching, asked the angel Gabriel, peace be upon him, who was present: 'O Gabriel, has the time of the noon prayer come?' Gabriel said: 'Yes.' The Messenger of God, upon whom be the most excellent of blessings, said: 'O Gabriel, what is the meaning of this?' Gabriel replied: 'O Messenger of God, you asked at a time when the sun had already completed five hundred thousand circuits of its orbit, and after that consider the disc of the moon, which receives light from the sun and serves as its deputy; but each night it diminishes, until it falls into conjunction, and after that consider...'

The sun in its vessel and the phases of its eclipse — when you look at it, it appears dark and then becomes capable of receiving light. And look: if the scholar of experience and practice seeks the way, the world will serve him; and note how the causes of things are explained — one should look carefully and consider the wonders. In the heavens and on earth, among the many phenomena: clouds forming, the rumbling of thunder, the flash of lightning, the formation of hailstones, the descent of rain in varied amounts — heavy and light — all come into being. In the clear air they are gathered and directed, the birds singing their melodies as they fly about. The droplets join together, drop by drop, until if they were strung like pearls they would be like a necklace poured out. If rain fell in excess of what is needed, it would ruin the lands and wash everything away; and if it fell short of what is needed, the plants could not bear fruit. The Holy Quran alludes to this where it says: 'And He who sends down water from the sky in due measure' [Q. 43:11]. Then look at the clouds: how they are formed, how they are driven about, how some of them produce rain or hail, how some gather moisture and are laden with it, how some scatter it, and how some dry up. And look at the variety of clouds: how they differ, how they yield their produce in so many ways. And look at the earth: how it is spread out as a vast carpet — a person could walk all his life without reaching its edges. As God says: 'And the earth — We spread it out; how excellent are We at spreading!' [Q. 51:48]. And consider dry ground — yet from it spring plants, minerals, and animals in wondrous variety. As God Most High says: 'Look then at the effects of God's mercy — how He gives life to the earth after its death.' [Q. 30:50]

Then after that, look at how around [this sea] the surrounding mountains shelter it like a tent, preventing [winds] from entering it. Then after that, the cold regions receded, so that rivers, caves, and grottoes filled with water, and the call to prayer rang out from within them. Then vegetation grew, and animals and plants came to exist until they reached their appointed time. Know that the waters and mountains came together, and look at how five [parts] remained. Then look at the wonders of its islands, which are like beautiful flowers of the archipelago, arrayed one beside another — five remain of it. Then look at the wonders of its creatures, for they are of marvelous forms — animals and creatures such that some have two bladders, and within them are living things, and creatures exist within them like monkeys, and [look at] their two bladders. And look further: within the shell of an oyster pearl forms, and trees like coral grow within it, and various kinds of precious stones are manifest — amber and rarities are apparent, and along the shore of the sea. And look: how small it seems, yet within the sea are wonders too numerous to be counted or comprehended. Then after that, look at the kinds of minerals: some are soft and suitable for compounding and making into gold, silver, copper, and clay; others are not suitable for softening and compounding — [such as] ruby, emerald, and turquoise. And look at the minerals, some of which yield naphtha and tar and the like. And consider how salt is produced: if the people of a city cannot obtain salt and eat their food without it, corruption spreads in that city. Then after that, look at the fruits and their varieties — how [they differ in] shape, like watermelons and cucumbers and other kinds — each produced from water, as God Most High has said: 
'And We have made some of them to excel others in [what they are good for as] food' (Quran 36:26 / cf. 13:4) — and from one seed many seeds are produced, as God Most High has declared.

If the soul controls itself, and if it is sound and free from desire and anger, it will attain perfection; otherwise it will not. Whoever escapes from these [passions] and maintains equilibrium — if the soul keeps itself pure and is established in what is required — then physical symptoms arise. If it is pure in the sense of being separated and self-subsistent, then symptoms arise at a given time, meaning [the soul] through knowledge and power
— that is, the concept in relation to something else, through rational comprehension —
and will, whether related to physical symptoms or not, whether divisible or not, whether it originated in that [state] or not, or whether it is related or not.
If its spatial relation results in the presence of something without [the soul], this is called 'Here.' If its temporal relation results in the presence of something, this is called 'When.' If the relation has no spatial component, this is called 'Relation.' If something exists in another through itself, this is called 'Being Acted Upon (an yanfa'il).' If something exists in another through the influence of one upon another — so long as it remains ordered — this is called 'Being Acted Upon.' If something encompasses another such that the encompassing thing moves by its movement, this is called 'Possession (milk).' If something is a substrate [for qualities], whether at rest or in motion, some [qualities] tending upward and some lateral, some in one direction and some in another, then in relation to the external reference point this is called 'Position (wad').' If it is conditioned by life or is dependent on inclination or volition, and if it is at rest, this is called 'Movement.' And if it is not at rest, this is called 'Perception (idrak).' If perception is also complete, then [it encompasses] the sciences and the arts, and ignorance; if it is partial, then perception is through the senses, conditioned by the sensory faculties without being limited to perceptible accidents. Through the faculty of sight, shapes and forms are perceived. Through the faculty of hearing, sounds are perceived. Through the faculty of smell, odors are perceived. Through the faculty of taste, flavors are perceived — nine categories. Through the faculty of touch, heat, cold, moisture, dryness, heaviness, and lightness are perceived.

And likewise, the angel, the owl, the ibis, and the desert road — none of these bear a proper relation or division. Among the categories of possible things mentioned in summary: Section — Let the companion travelers be mentioned. Among what is written in the journey, the right and lofty rank and the spiritual vision of the night. He first looked, and from that arose smoke rising upward — the Most High — and from that great treasure the names of the heavens were created. And He created the earth from its depths. To point to this, He says: 'Do those who disbelieve not see that the heavens and the earth were a joined entity, and We separated them?' [Quran 21:30]. And by this, the creation in six days is meant — that is, the creation took place over a period equivalent to six days. But before the creation of the heavens and the sun, there was no form, because a 'day' is reckoned by the rising and setting of the sun. Some scholars have said: on one day the matter of the earth was created, on the second day the form of the earth, on the third day the matter of the heavens, on the fourth day the form of the heavens, on the fifth day the completions of the earth — that is, mountains — and on the sixth day the adornments of the sky, namely the stars and souls, were created. Indeed, it is because everything that enters from below and rises up — as the Arabs say, 'whatever envelops, it covers' — and it is said that the sphere of the moon splits from the sphere. Regarding the earth, it is stated: 'Allah is He who created seven heavens and of the earth, the like of them.' [Quran 65:12]. The seven heavens are evident, but as for the seven earths, the author has explained this in several ways. The one he chose is this: the first sphere is fire, the second sphere is water, the third sphere is air, the fourth sphere is earth, and the uppermost layer — by the reckoning of their mixture — is in the middle layer. The first layer with the primordial matter is in flux. The third is air mixed with water. The fourth is produced from water and earth combined. And after that, the judge over the earth brings forth minerals.

...and of the plants and animals: this is what we have outlined in expounding all created things, and after mentioning it section by section, God willing — The Third Introduction: On the Meaning of the Strange (Gharīb)

A strange matter is one that occurs rarely, departing from custom, and is not produced by the influence of powerful souls, but rather proceeds from celestial affairs or elemental bodies, and God Most High has willed and ordained it thus.

Among these are the miracles of the Prophets, peace and blessings of God be upon them — that is, among the wonders are the miracles of the Prophets, peace be upon them: such as Muhammad, the Messenger of God (peace be upon him), splitting the moon; and Moses (peace be upon him), striking the sea so that it parted, and the staff that became a serpent; and how the great fire was made cool and safe for Abraham (peace be upon him); and Salih (peace be upon him) bringing forth a she-camel from solid rock; and Jesus (peace be upon him) giving life to the dead and healing the blind and the leper, and so on.

Among these also are the miraculous deeds (karamat) of the saints — may God sanctify their souls: those among them whose souls are so powerful that their influence appears beyond ordinary limits, such that if they wish, the sick are healed through their prayers, and plagues and pestilence, storms, rains, earthquakes, floods, fires, and many other events are averted by them; diseases and afflictions are repelled; great swarms of locusts and other creatures harmful to plants and animals are destroyed in a short time, as has occurred in many regions.

Anecdote: Abu al-Hasan ibn Bashir al-Jazari relates in his chronicle that in the year four hundred and [some] of the Hegira, a plague (bolt/pestilence) appeared in Ifriqiya (North Africa) — a strong and violent one — and after that, a great shower of stones fell, which sank ships; thus destruction came. And from there, heading toward the western regions of al-Safa, toward the city called Muristān and its surroundings, a plague appeared, from which...

Sounds without sound would be heard, and after that it would rain; hail would fall, people would take those fish from it, and the land of Ionia (Greece) would become dry. Among the wonders of the earth: we were told about the cities of Greece and their regions, and that the property of the Ionian land is such that nothing perishes there.

Merchants report that when one goes to that land, things remain on one's mind, and some go to sea and return. Among these wonders: those who were expert craftsmen would extract from the earthly phenomena what they needed, and from the shores of Egypt a sound would come from that place they call Nuhba, and that place they call Kayustum.

Among these: the earthquake of the city of Tibet and similar places — meaning from earthly phenomena, an earthquake occurred, producing a sound like smoke rising, and this was witnessed in the cities of Bur and Kark. — Anecdote — Sheikh Abu al-Qasim al-Rafi'i said: In the city of Qazvin there was a great earthquake; the roofs collapsed and people were killed. I saw stars and the sky, and afterward a bright crystal-clear fissure appeared.

Among these: the appearance of mineral deposits from the earth — meaning, from earthly phenomena, mineral deposits become apparent. It is reported that the Ismailis found gold appearing in their land.

Among these: the appearance of springs and streams at certain times from earthly phenomena — it is told that in the land of Sawa, in certain periods, plants would grow.

Among these: the birth of humans of strange forms from earthly phenomena — that is, humans being born of unusual shape...

A Strange Story: Imam al-Shafi'i, may God be pleased with him, has said: I once saw in a certain land a woman whose body from the waist upward was tall, with a small head and a different coloring to her eyes, and the women of that place would pull and push each other and sometimes there would be an uproar.

It is related that in the land of Balkh and Nawbandah there was a woman who gave birth to boys and girls alike, and she had half a light to her, and those who came to see her would marvel. This woman also gave birth to a girl with a head like a ram's, and it is said that this is a wondrous thing, for nothing comparable to it has been found. It was given no name. These first are of the traces of the carnal soul, and if the outward form proceeds from the saints, then it comes from the source; but if it proceeds from the base souls then it turns downward, for these strange matters come to pass through the influence of celestial bodies, and it is a particular mystery of their forms — and indeed these are among the wonders that the jinn are said to bring about in their totality.

[Marginal note, in red]: From the waist upward he described it as Adam, and below the waist as a Persian, as depicted [in the illustration].

This would be considered strange and remarkable speech by those who attribute it to the lodestone and its properties. As for its particulars, if they are mentioned, God willing, in the Fourth Premise on the Division of Existence — the existing things that God the Exalted has placed in creation to the extent found, whether in their substance, attributes, and qualities — from these come wonders and marvels, and the intellects are bewildered at His power in creating them. If mention of these is made in the manner described, it is necessary that existing things be divided into two parts: one part is that which human perception can grasp, as God the Exalted says: 'He creates what you do not know.' The second type is that which human sight and vision cannot perceive — such as the Throne, the Footstool, the angels, and the jinn — and this category is established only through proofs and evidences. The first category includes the heavens, the stars, the earth and what is within it, and what lies between the earth and sky. The wonders of each of these will be mentioned, God willing. In our book, from its introduction, each genus is divided into species, and each species is subdivided into varieties; and within each, there is wisdom, pointing to His uniqueness, His power, and His greatness. [Verse]: 'In every thing there is a sign pointing to His oneness' — a verse from the Throne to the earth, showing His power to every intelligent person. In no particle is there darkness that is not a sign of the Unique — look carefully, O perceiver, at every minute thing. There is not an atom but points to the Subtlety beyond it. After this, the table of contents of the book will be presented, showing that the two treatises: The First Treatise on Celestial Matters — and here the discussion and explanation of five matters follows.

The First Perspective ─── concerning the celestial spheres, their forms, configurations, movements, and sizes — their method. The Second Perspective: concerning the celestial sphere itself, what it contains; the First Chapter on the very essence of the sphere; the Second Chapter on the body of the sphere; in the Third [Chapter] on the increase and decrease of light; the Fourth Chapter on eclipses; the Fifth Chapter on the special properties of the sphere, and a conclusion. The Third Perspective: concerning the sphere of Mercury, what it contains — two chapters: the First Chapter on its sphere, the Second Chapter on its stars. The Fourth Perspective: concerning the sphere of Venus, what it contains — likewise two chapters: the First Chapter on its sphere, the Second Chapter on its stars. The Fifth Perspective: concerning the sphere of the Sun, what it contains — several chapters: the First Chapter on its sphere, the Second Chapter on the Sun itself, the Third Chapter on solar eclipses, the Fourth Chapter on the special properties of the Sun. The Sixth Perspective: concerning the sphere of Mars, what it contains — likewise two chapters: the First Chapter on its sphere, the Second Chapter on its stars. The Seventh Perspective: concerning the sphere of Jupiter, what it contains — likewise two chapters: the First Chapter on its sphere, the Second Chapter on its stars. The Eighth Perspective: concerning the sphere of Saturn, what it contains — likewise two chapters: the First Chapter on its sphere, the Second Chapter on its stars; and a final chapter on the retrograde motion of the planets and their direct motion. The Ninth Perspective: concerning the sphere of the fixed stars, what it contains — several chapters: the First Chapter on the spheres, the Second Chapter on their stars, the Third Chapter on the northern and southern constellations and their figures, the Fourth Chapter on the benefits of the northern and southern poles. The Tenth Perspective: concerning the sphere of the zodiacal signs in particular. The Eleventh Perspective: concerning the sphere above all spheres. The Twelfth Perspective: concerning the heavens, their inhabitants and what they contain. The Thirteenth Perspective: concerning time.

In this section there are also several chapters: in the first chapter, the reality of time; in the second chapter, the nights and days of the [year], ten in number; in the third chapter, the virtues of the [sacred] days and the days that are disliked, and their special properties; in the fourth chapter, the Arab years; in the fifth chapter, the Roman months; in the sixth chapter, the Persian years; in the seventh chapter, the months of the year; in the eighth chapter, the wonders related to the years. The Second Treatise concerns the Sublunary World, which contains five topics of inquiry. The First Topic: the Elements — here too there is one chapter: in the first chapter, the reality of the elements; in the second chapter, the transformation of some elements into others. The Second Topic: the Sphere of Fire — here too there is one chapter: in the first chapter, the reality of fire; in the second chapter, meteors and their naming. The Third Topic: the Sphere of Air — here too there are several chapters: in the first chapter, the reality of air; in the second chapter, clouds and rain; the third chapter, winds; the fourth chapter, thunder and lightning; the fifth chapter, thunderbolts and rainbows. The Fourth Topic: the Sphere of Water — here too there are several chapters: in the first chapter, the reality of water; in the second chapter, the sea, how it came to be and its location on one side of the earth; the third chapter, the seven seas; the fourth chapter, sea creatures. The Fifth Topic: the Sphere of Earth — here too there are several chapters: in the first chapter, the reality of the earth; in the second chapter, the descriptions of the earth; the third chapter, the size of the body of the earth; the fourth chapter, what lies above the earth; the fifth chapter, the seven climes; the sixth chapter, the accidents that befall the earth — earthquakes and sinkholes; the seventh chapter, [continuation].

Their valleys are white, their bodies are thick, and their natures are like the nature of beasts — they are raw and untamed. They are afflicted with misfortune and hardship. Their natures, properties, and influences are subject to the sun, standing at its edge, scorching and burning. It is claimed that three suns come together there, each one rising in a different town, so the entire celestial sphere consists of thirty-six units. It revolves thus, and the sun moves to the south of it, rising and shining. Settled places become ruined, and ruined places become settled; north becomes south and south becomes north. God knows best the particular wondrous and strange influences that occur there. It is based upon the noble Word of God Most High, which has been cited: 'On the Day when the earth shall be changed to another earth, and the heavens, and they shall appear before God, the One, the Overpowering' (Quran 14:48). It is as though this is sound speech, not merely a claim — by the will of God. Look:

Chapter Six

The First Chapter: On the Celestial Spheres and Their Arrangement

Each sphere contains within it another sphere. The outermost sphere is bounded, and its center is the center of the universe. On its upper surface it touches the sphere of the fixed stars, which encompasses all. Its contact with the sphere of the sun is from west to east, completing one full revolution every two days. The sphere of Mars and the sphere of the Moon resemble one another. If one goes inside, the spheres of the zodiac are arranged one within another, comprising seventy-eight degrees. 

Chapter: On the size of each sphere and its content

The smallest is Saturn; its description is given below. Its color is black and its nature is cold and dry. Its lords bring about corruption and destruction; its nature is harmful. Its distances and diameters: seventy-eight thousand and six hundred and thirty parasangs. And God knows best.

The Seventh Aspect: concerning the sphere of Jupiter. This contains two sections. The First Section concerns the entry of the sphere of Jupiter: its surface enters upon the upper surface of the sphere of Saturn, which is its highest surface, while the center of its lowest surface is the center of the world. Its center is the center of the universe, and its revolution is from west to east. Its revolution takes twenty-five degrees and twenty-five days to complete; according to one account, ten years, eleven months, and such-and-such days to complete the full revolution. The sphere of Jupiter resembles the sphere of Venus and the sphere of Venus likewise; its diagonal measure is approximately nine hundred and sixty-two thousand four hundred and two miles, and according to another account one thousand [miles]; the inclination is two hundred and ninety-two miles.

The Second Section: concerning Jupiter and its governance. Jupiter is a fortunate star, called the 'freezing of the pure.' It is pleasant and beneficial to the body; it is attributed with forms of goodness and great nobility. Jupiter is attributed to scholars, ministers, and the noble. The body of Jupiter has a settled rank: its third and quarter portions are fixed in the earth's diameter. Its sixth portion is fixed in the earth's diameter, and its daily motion is such-and-such minutes.

Whoever is informed of this and is capable of carrying it out will not deny it; another day will come, and those spheres will be of benefit to him. The bodies — those who know their measures will understand them, but the one who has comprehended this science will not find it far-fetched, for the wonders are beyond comprehension. Glory be to Him who made these subtle bodies and adorned them with these luminous celestial objects, and assigned to each of them what He willed, and gave mankind the faculty to perceive these obscure matters — 'and We have favored them over many of those We have created with great favor.' In particular, the science of the stars was made known through Idris (upon him be peace), and through what God revealed to him it became known; and indeed regarding the seven planets and the stars, generation after generation, it has been transmitted, and one who seeks satisfaction will find it. Thus the actions of those [planets] and the actions attributed to them have become known, and many weeks have passed in this manner, and when one takes this into account and refers to the time proportionally, it becomes evident.

[Planetary rulers:] Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, Sun, Moon, Mars

Other authorities have said that both day and night together make four hours for each [planet], and every hour that is even belongs to its planet, and for all fourteen hours, whoever is the lord of that color will be dominant therein.

Sunday Night: The first hour belongs to Mercury, and its treasure hour is the Moon — explained here within this scope.

When the hour is complete, it is not suitable to undertake a journey, to besiege and overwhelm, to begin an enterprise, or to seek a quarter and a watch. However, the people of fortune and prosperity will prevail, and things will become clear and bright. If one undertakes construction, he will find it sound; otherwise things will be broken and bitter. The balanced temperament will come, and he who is arrogant and self-deluded will be kept far away from benefit, while he who draws near will attain victory and success.

When the hour of [a certain celestial mansion] arrives, it is fitting to seek marriage, to perform talismans for attachment and the sight of women, to engage in intercourse, bloodletting, treatment, and bathing, to seek companionship, to speak kind words, and other such works.

But also: to place students in school, to begin instruction, and to raise children — for at this hour one who is born will grow up devoted to pleasure and joy; [they will be] of fair complexion, with clean face, dark eyes, small nose, hollow-cheeked, with proper eyebrows, graceful fingers, good-natured, affectionate, firm in friendship, sound in judgment, lover of music and perfume, accomplished, elegantly dressed, fond of good food, inclined toward composing fine verses. When the hour reaches the perfumer's station, it is fitting to send letters, to begin instruction in school for the first time, to seek talismans, and also for bloodletting, gathering, treatment, business, and marriage — at this hour children born will be fond of wholesome food, with bright eyes, well-formed limbs, and of good fortune. As for calculation and accounts, when the hour reaches [its station], it is beneficial for agriculture, property management, construction of gardens, beginning enterprises, increasing wealth, seeking good acquaintances and the sight of great men, and performing talismans to ward off enviers. Children born at this hour will be fair-complexioned, handsome of face, very observant, of good nature and fine life.

However, they will be devoid of generosity, excessively miserly, deceitful, and quarrelsome.

When the hour of [another mansion] arrives, it is fitting to perform marriage, undertake enterprises, engage in agriculture, construction, business, making talismans, buying and selling, and eating good food. Children born at this hour will be fond of wholesome food, but with a stern character, somewhat coarse-faced, frowning of countenance, and prone to outbursts.

Few in speech, and benefiting from the miser and the envious, and the foolish-natured people mixing — do not spend your whole life on this. The goods of this world — he has no share of them. At that hour, it is not appropriate to seek needs, perform phlebotomy, cupping, travel, or visit the regions of kings, or to buy and sell, or to seek marriage and request favors, or to travel to distant regions and small villages, and to perform phlebotomy and cupping — it is not appropriate at this time. To cause corruption and those who spread corruption — look, at that hour, the white-faced, the clear-eyed, the pure-faced, the forty-companioned, the colorful, the great, the well-used, the amusement and singing lovers, the seekers of requests, the wise, the prudent, the people of virtue — do not indicate to any one person, and do not make anyone a target of indication, and it is lawful to incline toward companionship and to travel and see good fortune, for that is the best way to achieve one's aim, and to make talismans against enemies, to perform phlebotomy and cupping — it is not appropriate at this time, to visit kings and nobles, to seek needs and favors, and to buy and sell. At that hour, those who appear are straightforward, from a village, bold and mighty, long-necked, eating unlawfully, causing strife, doing harm, and people-harassing, and among the worst companions — they will come out quarrelsome, selfish, covetous. As for the celestial sphere and the angels, and the ordering of the heavens and the events that have been recorded — know that the reason for the descent of the planets and their association with the seven climes: each of the seven planets is connected to one of the seven climes. The first clime belongs to Saturn; the first lands are under it. In the second clime, Jupiter is ascribed; the first land is Azerbaijan. In the third clime, Mars is ascribed; the first lands belong to it. In the fourth clime — the first lands of Khurasan are ascribed. In the fifth clime, the Sun is ascribed. The first lands beyond the river [Transoxiana] are in the sixth clime, Mercury is ascribed, and the first lands of Rum [Anatolia/Byzantium] are in the seventh clime, which is assigned [to the Moon].

The first of the lands of the Bulgars is Balkak (Bulghar). It is the greatest city, situated on the bank of the great river (Volga) and the smaller river. When all the planets are in conjunction in one degree, it signifies intense cold; and when they are spread two degrees apart, it signifies moderate cold; when most of them are gathered in one degree, it signifies burning heat; when they are in one degree with the seven stars, the particular positions of each star become effective—their whiteness indicates benefit and their brightness indicates an example. When they are in opposition, trine, or sextile, the rulings apply. First I will mention the aforementioned positions, then secondly I will mention the rulings. When a planet reaches thirty degrees in the zodiac sign below it, that is its sextile; when it reaches sixty degrees, that is its trine; when it reaches ninety degrees below the sign of Aries, that is its square; when it reaches one hundred twenty degrees, that is its trine of Bozkiri; when it reaches one hundred fifty degrees, that is its opposition of Bozsoksan (180 degrees); when a planet reaches double its sign and there are no degrees, that is its conjunction—when two planets come together in the same degree and minute, they are said to be in conjunction. Now I will explain the rulings concerning the positions of the Moon, Saturn, and Jupiter together: when the Moon is in their degree, it is good for seeking needs, buying and selling servants and slaves, purchasing salt, cupping (bloodletting), eating meat, and hiring workers; it is also good for possessing kingdoms, farming, planting palms, planting trees, and visiting elders. If it is a square aspect, it is good for travel, movement, beginning work and construction. If it is a trine, it is good for building, cutting wood, going to the baths, visiting hammams, construction, and acquiring servants.

And if [the Moon is] in Virgo (al-ملق) and in conjunction, it is auspicious for all movements, actions, and seeking of needs; and if [it is] at the beginning, it is good for the affairs of the common people, lawsuits, bloodletting, cupping, and dental extraction. It is good for travel in particular; [in] the Pleiades conjunction it is good for scholars and judges. And for legal religious claims, if [the Moon] is in its direct course, it is good for the initiation of deeds, marriage, collecting debts, and commerce. And if [it is] in spring, it is good for claiming rights and disputes. And if [it is] in the waning phase, it is good for travel, correspondence with kings and officials, and the initiation of affairs. And if [it is] in opposition, it is good for claiming inheritance and lawsuits. If [the Moon is in] Mars conjunction, it is auspicious for all movements, initiation [of affairs], and seeking of needs — except for cunning and politics. If [the Moon] is in its direct course, it is good for bloodletting, cupping, warfare, military campaigns, hunting, nail-cutting, and hair removal. And if [it is] in spring, it is good for travel, movement, construction, and beginning of work and trade. In every [matter] one must be careful lest an enemy intend harm. And if [it is] in the waning phase, it is good for hunting, warfare, seeking employment, riding, and hunting. And if [it is] in opposition, it is good for travel, movement, and initiation of work — except that weapons should be put in order. [If the Moon is in] Sun conjunction, it is good for all work except sending spies and carrying news. And if [it is] in direct course, it is good for meeting with nobles, attaining office, and initiating great written works. And if [it is] in spring, it is good for travel, movement, and initiating great enterprises. And if [it is] in the waning phase, it is good for work and seeking of needs. And if [it is] in meeting with nobles and in opposition, it is good for all affairs — except imprisonment is [still] auspicious.

If the enemies' [planet] is in conjunction with Qin [Jupiter?], travel, movement, marriage, and music occur. If it produces a trine, it indicates meeting women, servants, adornment, and the beginning of matters. If it forms a square, it indicates building, travel, movement, slaves, and servants. If it forms a trine with Saturn, it indicates marriage, seeking needs, and beginning of work. If it is in opposition, it indicates war, the beginning of matters, and matters concerning women and pleasure. If Mercury forms a conjunction with it, it indicates learning writing, musical science, and the beginning of sciences, solving problems, accounting, meeting people. If it forms a sextile, it indicates hunting, selling livestock, playing chess, and removing needs. If it forms a square, it indicates riding, playing polo, sending messengers and letters, companionship, and accounting. If it forms a trine, it indicates meeting with ministers, writing, accounting, seeking gifts, learning, and selling. If it is in opposition, it indicates disputes, quarreling, debate, military training, and the nightingale [lulbulak sign].

The seven planets: Saturn is cold and dry in nature; Jupiter is warm and moist; Mars is warm and dry; the Sun is warm and dry; Venus is mostly moist; Mercury is variable according to what it joins with; the Moon is cool and moist.

As for the people born under each [planet]: some are masculine and some feminine, and some are mixed. Saturn is masculine; Jupiter is masculine; Mars is considered masculine by day and feminine by night; the Sun repeats [its nature]; Venus is feminine; Mercury is variable; the Moon [follows].

The nightingale [lulbulak] and Marluzak: in their conjunction the rulings and judgments have a basis, and here I explain them briefly so that the reader may not err and may come to understand.

The conjunction (qiran) of Saturn and Jupiter: If it occurs in Aries, it indicates corruption spreading across the eastern lands and Khurasan, and in Rum and the surrounding regions — wars and conflicts breaking out between rulers, and incidents of burning and looting occurring. Among diseases, headaches and scalp ailments will spread. If the conjunction occurs with both planets in good condition, it indicates that rulers will deal justly with their subjects and the people will incline toward obedience.

The conjunction of Saturn and Jupiter: If it occurs in Taurus, it indicates the destruction of many four-legged animals, corruption among rulers, their undertaking of journeys, the occurrence of powerful epidemics, the death of women, and trouble in the lands beyond the river (Transoxiana) and in Ferghana. If the conjunction occurs with both planets — Venus and Jupiter — in a favorable configuration, it indicates abundance and prosperity, while also signaling increased brigandry, the death of livestock, humiliation of the powerful, conflict and enmity, the ruin of towns, the disruption of noble lineages and dynasties, the spread of ill repute, and the destruction of four-legged animals — their numbers falling and harmful things settling upon the settlements.

The conjunction of Saturn and Jupiter: If it occurs in Gemini, it indicates hardship in the western lands, along the northern frontiers, and in the cities of Rum and the surrounding areas — corruption among the people, scarcity of wealth and provisions, the appearance of signs, harm to the inhabitants, and destruction of four-legged animals. If the conjunction occurs with Mercury in a good configuration, it indicates loss to the people, disruption of the journeys and movements of merchants, corruption of their affairs, disobedience of soldiers toward the ruler, destruction of prices, and a decline in the markets.

The conjunction of Saturn and Jupiter: If it occurs in Cancer, it indicates events in Armenia, the Arab lands, the region of Iraq, Khurasan, and along the frontiers of the infidels — increased hardship and difficulties, a decline in cavalry, and corruption of the conditions of those who travel for profit (usurers/merchants).

And the conjunction of the planets in [the sign of] Sagittarius, if it occurs there, indicates war and strife breaking out in Turkestan, the Arab lands, and Khorasan, and oppression falling upon the subjects by rulers, and the appearance of celestial signs such as fire and lightning, and the occurrence of earthquakes, and widespread corruption and destructive heat, and the ruin of merchants. If the conjunction occurs in both sides [of the sign], it indicates wars among kings and mutual slaughter. The conjunction in Virgo indicates: the outbreak of deadly wars in the lands of Egypt, the Arab and Persian lands, an abundance of pestilence in a short time, the spread of plague, scarcity of rain, suffering of the poor, and the occurrence of calamities. If Mercury is in a good state, it indicates the blossoming of merchants. If the Sun bears witness [is in aspect], it indicates the increase of oppressors, confiscation of wealth from the rich, and their extortion. The spread of adultery and fornication becoming public. The conjunction in Libra indicates: the outbreak of strife in the western lands, the Arab territories, and the cities of Anatolia (Rum), plundering, and kings seizing [wealth] greedily; the corruption of women, the indifference of the wealthy, deflection of harm, and the occurrence of famine; the appearance of signs of death, the decline and collapse of kingdoms. If Mercury or Jupiter bears witness [is in aspect], it indicates the corrupt state of the wicked and the depraved. If Venus bears witness, it indicates the corrupt state of married women and their death. If the Moon bears witness, it indicates the oppression of kingdoms and the suffering of subjects, destitution among the people, and the ruin of the populace. The conjunction in Scorpio indicates: the outbreak of war and strife in the western lands, on the seas, and near the seas.

And altogether, the signs of the zodiac (falak al-buruj) are divided into two parts — each part is called a 'group,' and each group's signs are arranged in order, as stated in the verse:

Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, and Leo • Virgo of summer, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces.

And each zodiac sign occupies one-twelfth of the celestial sphere; that is, the sphere of the zodiac is divided among the twelve signs, and each sign spans thirty degrees — for each degree is one-twelfth of the ecliptic circle, which amounts to three hundred and sixty degrees in total, and twelve times thirty is three hundred and sixty.

Cancer, Leo, and Virgo are the summer signs; and Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, and Aquarius are the winter signs. The sun traverses one sign per month, and in one year it passes through two solstices and two equinoxes. The northern side is called 'north' and the southern side is called 'south.' The great circle known as the ecliptic (mantiqa al-buruj) is also called the zodiac belt.

The signs are grouped by triangles (trigons/triplicity), by squares (quadruplicity), and by sextiles (sextile aspect).

The first triangle is the Fire trigon: the first is Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius — each of whose compound nature is hot and dry.
The second triangle is the Earth trigon: the first is Taurus, Virgo, and Capricorn — each of whose compound nature is cold and dry.
The third triangle is the Air trigon: the first is Gemini, Libra, and Aquarius — each of whose compound nature is hot and moist.
The fourth triangle is the Water trigon: the first is Cancer, Scorpio, and Pisces — each of whose compound nature is cold and moist.

Among the cardinal (movable) signs of the upper sphere are: Aries, Cancer, Libra, and Capricorn. Among the fixed signs of the lower sphere are: Taurus, Leo, Scorpio, and Aquarius. Among the mutable (common) signs of the upper sphere are: Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius, and Pisces.

And below, in the middle: in the First [degree], the hexagonal signs are Aries, Gemini, Leo, Libra, Sagittarius, and Aquarius — these are the signs from which the luminaries of the celestial sphere draw fiery and airy [qualities]; and in the Second [degree] are Taurus, Virgo, Scorpio, and Pisces — from these the light is diminished, because these are watery and earthy signs. Moreover, it should be known that Aries and Scorpio are the house of Mars; Taurus and Libra the house of Venus; Gemini and Virgo the house of Mercury; Sagittarius and Pisces the house of Jupiter; Capricorn and Aquarius the house of Saturn; Leo the house of the Sun; and Cancer the house of the Moon. And it should further be known that each sign is divided into faces [decanates] according to the Ptolemaic system, and by considering the degrees of exaltation and fall, one determines to which sign a place belongs.

These are the degrees [of planetary dignity]. In Aries: the degree of Mercury's exaltation; the Sun and Venus in Taurus; Mercury, Moon, and Saturn in Gemini; Venus and Jupiter in Cancer; the Sun and Saturn in Leo; Mercury and Jupiter and Mars in Virgo; the Sun, Venus, and Mercury in Libra; Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn in Scorpio; Mercury, Moon, and Saturn in Sagittarius; Venus and Mercury in Capricorn; Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars in Aquarius; and in Pisces — and in sum, of all seven planets, the stars' joy: Saturn's joy is in Capricorn, Jupiter's joy is in Sagittarius, Venus's joy is in Taurus [nineteen degrees of joy], Mars's joy is in Aries, Mercury's joy is in Virgo, the Sun's joy is in Leo, and the Moon's joy is in Cancer. Now since these seven planets' conditions and technical terms of astrology are to be presented, and the words belong to those who know the science of the spheres and the properties of the planets, I will first explain certain conditions of the fixed stars, that is, the magnitudes of the fixed stars. They are compared [to one another], some being larger and some smaller. Therefore the scholars of the science of the [stellar] magnitudes have established the following: The first magnitude consists of those stars which, when observed, are the greatest in appearance, and those a little smaller than these are of the second magnitude; those a little smaller than these are of the third magnitude; those a little smaller than these are of the fourth magnitude; those a little smaller than these are of the fifth magnitude; and those a little smaller than these are of the sixth magnitude — thus they have established this terminology. Stars of the first magnitude are as large as [a city's chief governor]; stars of the second magnitude are like [district governors]; stars of the third magnitude are like [town heads]; stars of the fourth magnitude are like [village headmen]; stars of the fifth magnitude are like [hamlet leaders]; stars of the sixth magnitude are like [household heads] — and of these...

A session: with one good star in it, and expelling outside those four stars of the south — entering into the hidden ones. The small ones in the nine hidden [stars], as Ptolemy organized and arranged, concerning the noble houses, taking two. It becomes two, and beginning to speak of the category of stars — Chapter: on the explanation of the fixed stars. The number of fixed stars is more than what can be precisely determined; rather, from their totality one takes two or three. They have been registered [by astronomers], so that now we mention them, and we recount some of their forms — figures that contain the stars of their regions, as Ptolemy recorded in his book the Almagest. Some are in the northern half, and some are on the ecliptic — the path of the planets — and some are in the southern half. Some figures resemble a tongue, as [a constellation] completing a quadrant figure. Some animals appear in the form of Cancer and the like, and some animals appear in a single form, like [Aquila] the Eagle, and some like a scale without a tongue [i.e., Libra], and some resemble a tongue or flat surface, as completed by Pisces [lit. 'the horse's piece'], and some from pools — some of them on one side, some on the other far side with a portion. Some of these forms are not fully complete until the other forms come close to them — understand this, and memorize the problem. And these figures: the ancients listed them, [the book] of stars mentioning them: these are the stars, others are their stars, and when counting stars — mentioning that a certain figure is at a certain member, in the north above the ecliptic or above the ecliptic or in the south — then the listener benefits and understands. When [a star] rises, and Venus appears, and it becomes clear at night in the stars and in their ecliptic regions — and whichever figure it is near, of those figures, it is close to it and resembles it.

Among the types [of stars]: those that are said to be outside the figure (constellation), beyond what is counted as belonging to it — these are called 'extra' stars. The third [chapter] speaks of the stars of Ursa Major (al-Dubb al-Akbar). The pole star is above the head [of the Bear], and [the constellation] is in the north. There are twelve [signs] in the ecliptic (mintaqat al-buruj), fifteen [constellations] in the southern celestial sphere, and [the rest] in the northern. The fixed stars of each constellation are enumerated: the first [constellation] to be described is the one whose stars lie outside the main figure — those to the north are mentioned first. They are arranged in order of their positions: some [stars] together number twenty-two, [for example] Gemini (Jawza') has thirty-two [stars]. Those stars of the northern side that belong to the figure of al-Muthallath (the Triangle) — [the section begins with] Ursa Minor (al-Dubb al-Asghar), which is near the northern pole; its stars [forming] the body of the figure number seven. Those [stars] outside the figure, on the western side, are the Daughters of the Bier (Banat Na'sh). The first three of those stars are called al-Farkadan, and the next star after them is called Farkad, and the one [star] called al-Jad'r. They indicate the direction of the qibla, and [the text says] the pole is at a certain elevation — and God knows best.

Second figure: I turn from the constellation of Ursa Major — among those stars found in this figure, they say there are eight stars outside the figure. The first four stars are like a quadrilateral; they are called the stretcher (bier), and the three stars over the ribs are called the daughters of the bier (Banat al-Na'sh). The star at the tip of the ribs — in it there is a benefit — the middle star is called 'Anaq, and the star near the end of the figure is called Quraina. Below it they call it Hayun. Over 'Anaq there is a small faint star; they call it its kid (al-'Anaq's kid). People test their eyesight with it. When you look at it, say: 'I seek refuge with the bright one (Suhayl) from every scorpion and serpent' — meaning all venomous creatures. Among the feet of the figure are the Leaps of the Gazelles (Qafazat al-Ziba); some call them Farqah. The leap in which the gazelle stands on its right foot — that star is called Nabi', and the other Qahrf. These stars are over the ribs of each lion, and the Arabs say: 'The gazelles of the earth have fled.' Those stars over the eyes, the brows, the ears, and the nose represent gazelles. A lion frightens them away; they leap from their watering place (Hawd), scatter in all directions, and those stars are collectively called Balnaba. The middle star — of the two that rise together at the same time — the brighter one they call the Liver of the Lion (Kabid al-Asad). The six stars near the fifth approximation and after it — some call them Ziba (gazelles) and some call them Taqlisa and Uladziba. As for Ursa Major: it is a great bear in form, standing on its four legs, with its neck stretched out and its ribs extended, its arms spread wide like a human, it is said.

The Third Figure: Ursa Minor (or the Bear Cub)

The Third Figure: This is the figure of the Bear Cub (Ursa Minor). Among the stars that the Arabs call those upon its head — on the opposite side there are four stars. Apart from these, upon its body there are stars, and at its end there is one star. It is small, and there are two stars like a camel upon it, and the first of these stars is bright, and at the end of Ursa Minor's tail there are ten stars in the sea. The first of these stars among them — the brightest two stars — are brilliant, and they are found at the extremities of the tail, and beyond them there are faint stars.
The movement of the constellation has the meaning of change and transformation in its nature, so take heed.

The Figure of the Great Sea (Cetus / the Sea Monster)

The Fourth Figure [Ophiuchus/Serpentarius]: Regarding the image of the fourth figure called Qiqawus [Ophiuchus], it resembles a man dancing, with something like a cap upon his head. Both hands are raised, and the figure is described as wrestling. There are two stars along its form that differ from the others, and outside the constellation there are stars on its right shoulder called Qifri, and on its left shoulder above, and stars on the lower parts named after a shepherd's crook, and behind its feet there are small stars called the Flock.

The Fifth Figure [Boötes]: Regarding the image of the fifth figure called 'Awwa' [Boötes], it is depicted as a man standing upright, holding a staff. He stands in the image with both arms raised, staff in hand. The stars of this figure include those within the constellation and those outside it, on both sides. It is said that when a person has a pterygium (ẓafara) in their eye, they should look toward the South Pole and toward Canopus (Suhayl). If it begins during the month of Virgo (Sunbula), it will be completely gone within forty-nine nights.

Altogether, there are twenty-eight lunar mansions in detail. Let me explain so that the principle becomes known, and here is the detail of that principle:

The Arabs and desert dwellers, since ancient times, reckoned their calendar by the appearance of the crescent moon. But this system proved inconsistent — sometimes falling in summer, sometimes in winter. In order to properly regulate the solar year, they adopted solar reckoning so they could know the seasons of the year. In relation to these seasons, they needed to attend to pasturelands and wintering grounds, staying in their lowland pastures when appropriate. They needed to observe the conditions overhead, and they found that the celestial sphere passes over a fixed number of days and nights per segment. They saw that in two nights at the end of a month the moon becomes invisible; accordingly they dropped those nights from the count and divided the visible circuit of the celestial sphere into twenty-eight parts. Each part they called a mansion (manzil), and they said the moon occupies one of these mansions each night. They assigned a marker to each mansion so that one could be distinguished from another, and the scholars of the stars called this the "path of Qarah-Qar" [i.e., the method of Karokar/the zodiacal belt]. Of these twenty-eight mansions, fourteen rise in the east and set: sometimes they rise in the east and set in the west, some rising while others set, and fourteen are grouped as the "harmful" ones (manāzil al-ḍarr). Those that rise in the dawn and set in the evening set in the west while the opposite ones rise in the east. It ends with [the mansions of] al-Safar, al-Fargh, al-Qanb, al-Mughrib, al-Sāwila, and al-Bald.

...and from cold and frost. And when the lunar mansion is complete, it appears just as its equal and counterpart, and they are called the mansions of al-Sharatain. The last of them is al-Ghafr, and the first mansion is Nath, and when these mansions rise in the east and set in the west, this is a matter that cannot be fully understood in one year. Rather, know that the celestial sphere is divided into twelve parts, and the division of the zodiacal belt is into houses, and the division of its middle circle is into twenty-eight lunar mansions, and they are called the mansions of the stars. The difference between them is that the zodiacal houses are determined by the passage of the sun — as it were, the stars of the fixed mansions are arranged in order — and those are: "That is the decree of the Mighty, the Knowing" [Quran 36:38]. Thus the Almighty God, exalted and glorified, created these things, and so the point of the equinox moves through each of the zodiac signs, and the lunar mansions of al-Sharatain occur, and they are close to the ecliptic, and they are called the first mansion — "Shadalankaro" and the mansions of Kasil — with their aspects and some of their states and some of their forms and some of their conditions, as is well-known among them: al-Sharatain. This station is sometimes called elevated and sometimes base, and it is called "Sharatan" in the sense of a sign or mark, meaning a sign for conditions and indications of states. Its two stars are located near the Pleiades, and they are faint and close together, spanning about one thousand units in measure. Their shadows fall to the north in the southern direction, and when the sun is among them at the two equinox seasons, they become equal. And when al-Sharatain rises, the parts of time become equal. Their counterpart star is light and swift in motion. These are to be considered as reference points for al-Sirat, and their form is thus: ••••• And the rising of this mansion...

When the color of the human being is at this point, it falls; when the Pleiades (Nathrah) rise in the eighth [station], it produces a kind of wonder. It disappears in time and its waters rise, and images increase, and it produces various types of bounty. The smallest of its forms settles in the belly, as is described: it is reckoned below the belly in proportion to the smallest. The hidden stars at that point, three of them appearing like stones — their foot-shape becomes apparent. When one night before Libra (Qalinji) rises, and one night before the beginning of Tishrin (October) has passed, one night of Libra's season — if the falling [of rain] does not occur, the descendants will be in distress, and kites and buzzards will come to the coasts, and ants will emerge from under stones. A kind of wonder is noted: when it is as if the sands are washed and the redness goes and the Arabs call these phenomena 'al-Anwa' (the star-rains). At its time, the winds blow and the streams run, and its setting and rising are well known. At that point, al-Hamal (Aries) ascends, and it is known that when it is in the middle, small grains scatter, and the observers say it is beyond telling. When many stars appear, or when rain falls at that time, abundance comes, meaning prosperity increases — this is according to the smallest of the Pleiades (Thurayya al-Sughra). The other form of it is that when it is plentiful, it means much wealth — that is its other form. So when it rises in the third part of Tishrin al-Akhir (late October) and falls, and when it rises in the east from Misr (Egypt), winter becomes apparent. And one night, the cold of mid-autumn comes, and winter remains and the rains come. Its rising is blessed, as the Prophet of God — peace be upon him — said: 'When the Pleiades rise, harm departs from every people.' That is, when the Pleiades (Thurayya) rise, calamity departs and the Arabs say this kind of wonder — rain after its rising is very beneficial, because the earth absorbs it and stores moisture within it, and what comes after the rising of the Pleiades: winter becomes apparent among the Arabs, as it is said: 'When the Pleiades rise, the seas surge and the winds clash and the sultan [of storms rules].'

The jinn dwell upon the waters. During the season of the Pleiades, the air becomes pleasant, the terrain becomes traversable, and horses thrive; toward its end, the Nile rises and sailors' livelihoods improve. Between them the rulings and stable observations are to be noted, and they are matched in their phase. The Lesser Bear rises in one position and sets in Adhar in another position. The chief Mahmud brings much rain; orchards become cool, moisture increases, and its companion is in the Hadi position, and its second letter follows. This appears in the Lesser Burj when it reaches Zuhra; its form appears. This Moon is in the opposition of Zuhra; the heart of Leo disperses coldness and its setting disperses heat toward Leo. 

The rising is in the month of Elul, on the third day, and the setting is in the month of Adhar in the first days, and its days grow cold as Naylaart returns, and the companion is Fara' Muqaddam, and its pair is 'Awa — in exchange and proportion. Its meaning relates to the positions of the stars; the word 'Lam' means that no one among Naʿm and Bala in its direction... They settled in Kalbalde, sent toward Arslan, gathered against them, and it is called so. The rising is on the twenty-eighth of Elul and the setting is on the twenty-eighth of Adhar, and the chief Mahmud — its companion is Fara' Mu'akhkhar and its fourth is Sak, and this is Sak, the single 'Azl.

Without its counterpart [i.e., Unoccupied / solo], near Tawnak, there is no smoky star; however, near the Spear-bearer Simak (Arcturus), there is a smoky star. That smoky star is between the two, between the Unarmed Simak and the Spear-bearing Simak, standing roughly equidistant. Its form is that of a figure. • The rising of Tawnak is at the end of the first decade of Tishrin (October), and its setting is on the fourth of Nisan (April). Its nature is powerful; it rarely occurs with pestilence or harm. And the twenty-seventh [mansion] is al-Ghafr — with a fatḥa on the ghayn and sukūn on the fāʾ — meaning its opposite; it consists of three dim stars in the constellation Virgo. •• They call it al-Ghafr (the cover/concealment) because its rising coincides with the great star Mizar becoming hidden from sight, growing distant, and the Ghafr stars themselves are dim stars hidden from observation, growing distant. Its rising is on the twenty-eighth of Tishrin (October) and its setting is on the sixteenth of Nisan (April). Its nature is that of Sharṭā. The twenty-eighth mansion is al-Zubānā — with a fatḥa on the zāʾ, meaning 'the claws' — and the two stars of it are like Tir (Mercury); they are called the horns of Scorpio. Their number in Karshakar's reckoning is [given]. • Its rising is at the end of Tishrin (October) and its setting is at the end of Nisan (April). Under its nature, the people of the settled lands and the surrounding regions enter into difficulties and hardship. The twenty-ninth mansion is al-Iklīl (the Crown), meaning its opposite; it consists of four stars forming the head of Scorpio, and it is also called the other Karshakar. • Its rising falls in the eighth of Tishrin (October) and its setting is on the tenth of Bārkil (November); under its nature, horses wander until the belly of Ḥūt (Pisces) rises, and horses are not found. The twenty-eighth [star] is Qalb [al-Aqrab] (Heart of the Scorpion): a single bright star, and near it are two other stars also called Ṣanw, one of which is somewhat above and the other somewhat below.

Its shape is thus: It is called Qalb al-Aqrab [Heart of the Scorpion]. Its heliacal rising occurs on the sixth day of the last Tishrin [November], and its setting is on the sixth day of Iyar [May]. Its benefit is well-known: if one reaches that water it dries up. Its opposing star is in Diran, the twenty-ninth [star], which is called Shawl, in Fitshan, and it runs along.

The meaning of 'Scorpio's depth': In it there are stars close together, resembling one another — for this reason it is called 'the strength of Scorpio.' Therefore it appears elevated in the north, below Thawr [Taurus], and its shape is thus. Its rising is on the twenty-second of Kanun al-Awwal [December], and its setting occurs on the first days of the entering of Iyar [May]. Its benefit for that vicinity is that trees produce fruit, pastures grow, and orchards bear. Its opposing star is of great benefit, the second [in rank]. It is called the name for a camel's growl. And the ninth of the sheep's orbit is called thus, and these seven stars are exactly opposite the Milky Way. In it the melodies that arrive are said to be from the Milky Way; the melodies that issue out are said to come from what exits the Milky Way. The melodies proceeding are said to be below [the track of] the Milky Way, having emerged from beneath it, just as the outer [stars] resemble the shape of a bowl.

Its shape is thus: ... Its rising is on the twenty-fifth of Kanun al-Awwal [December], and its setting is on the twenty-fifth of entering Iyar [May]. Its benefit in that period: days and nights become equal, and its opposing star is of benefit, the twentieth [in rank], a gift. Hope arises and the melodies dissipate and are lost. There is no star in the Milky Way [at this point]; a faint star appears there. It goes with Kawch [?] in Libra and some stars are in Qaws [Sagittarius] in that manner, and its shape appears thus.

.... Its rising is at the end of Kanun al-Akhir [late January], and its setting is at the end of Tawz [Tammuz/July]. In its period of benefit, the twenty-sixth [star] is Sa'd Dhabih [the Lucky Stars of the Slaughterer]. In it small stars appear at its setting. From it, toward the north by about one cubit, no star appears along the Milky Way, but to the south there are rays in the direction of the south.

And among the small stars that appear in Arabia, there are sheep — that is what they call this asterism. Its form resembles that. Its heliacal rising is on the seventeenth of the last month of winter (Kanun al-Akhir), and its setting is on the seventeenth of Tammuz. In its season the trees draw up water, Adam-trees and Zughaj-trees begin to move, and its mansion is Nathrah.

The second and third [star] is Sa'd al-Dhabi': it moves through the sky equal to the greater [star] and surpasses it. Its form is like the greater Suhail of the south, and one may call it the eraser. Its form is thus. From this point it is named Nizam. When it rises in the middle of the last Kanun, on the twenty-ninth day of that month it sets; and when it sets, in the month of Ab on its twenty-ninth. In its season onions, garlic, and meats grow strong, and salt, good things, and wind come from the south; its mansion faces Tarfah, and the second and third is Sa'd al-Su'ud. The sum of its stars: the seven of the Crown — such is its form. The source of its provision is Nizam, the source of its people and their livelihood, and the Arabs call this auspicious, giving food for its sake, therefore it is named. Its rising is on the twenty-second of Shubat and its setting on the fourteenth of Ab. The stars are gathered, and all the trees shed their leaves; starlings come, storks return from Rum, monks withdraw, and the days shorten.

The fifth [asterism] is Sa'd al-Akhbiyah: it lies in all directions, four stars like a hunter's form — thus. Its naming is Nizam.

When the red [stars] move in the land of desolation, for that reason it is named, therefore. Its rising is on the twenty-fifth of Shubat and its setting on the fourth of Ab. Its season is gathered thus: buffaloes drink water, chains are cut, its mansion is Zubarah, and the second is al-Tabani. Here, read and ponder — here, ponder the introduction of Fargh.

And another [star group] called Farghana: it is said to be among the mansions of the lunar stations, and its stars are each about five cubits apart in appearance, resembling a form without clear shape.
They are used as a guide for travelers, for when they rise and set they indicate [the seasons]. Their rising is in the sign of Aries [Hamal], and their number is nine and twenty [29], and their setting occurs on the twenty-ninth [day], and within it are certain winds and vapors.
And its dome [culmination] is in the direction of Qara, and when Aries rises in the season called Akis [harvest time], and sets in Akis [the same], its culmination occurs in that period, and in it are hot winds called Shadar and Fughaa and Ragham.
This [mansion] is close to the Fish [Pisces], and when the constellation of the Fish [Hut] reaches its belly, it indicates that from the direction of the south, the star Shatir rises with it, and this signifies the occurrence of cold and the approach of winter.
As for its rising, it is on the fourth of Nisan [April], and its setting is on the fifth of Tishrin [October], and thereafter the nights grow longer and the days begin to shorten, and the stars called Balkak appear.
Abu Ishaq [the astronomer] says: its journey through the signs is seven [degrees] per mansion, and each mansion has ten stars [kawkab], and one of them, namely Jabba, exceeds [this]. It completes [its course] in sixty-five days, and the sun traverses the Greek [Roman] celestial sphere in that time. The Balkak [Pleiades] are well-known mansions, more recognized and familiar than [other] mansions among travelers.
Know that the first of the Niza [lunar mansion markers] is a road leading to the treasury [Khazina], and from there seek [the next]. In that celestial sphere, on the northern side, go one day's measure and then seek the Two Conditions [Shartayn]. Then from that celestial sphere go westward one day's measure and from there seek Butayn. Then [go] toward the mansion Niza, and the Two Conditions, note well.

After the rank of these mansions has been established, one becomes able to understand the remaining mansions — indeed, like the path of the moon. Regarding the eastern and western regions, it is not a simplification to say that the mansions pass through each zodiac sign in a certain number of nights. It was mentioned in Tawqaruda that sometimes it passes through the eight mansions quickly and sometimes slowly — sometimes completing half the day's distance in one mansion, sometimes reaching the third mansion by midday, sometimes completing a mansion in half a day, and sometimes at midday it falls short by a fraction. When the celestial sphere divides into twelve zodiac signs, or sometimes into twenty-eight mansions proportionally, each zodiac sign receives its share of the mentioned mansions — one mansion, or a third of a mansion, and so on. When the moon passes through the mentioned mansions, it is as Ibn Ali indicated, and Ibn Ali also explained this elsewhere. Since it is of general benefit and complete utility, we mention it line by line, for when the moon is in:
