The Tenth View: The Sphere of the Zodiac is in the form of the Sphere of the Signs, which is an independent sphere, unlike the other spheres. Rather, it has been mentioned that each star has its own dedicated sphere, and each sphere has two poles. Since each sphere revolves around its center, the first star revolves around the center of its sphere from which the result comes, and the star moves from east to west as the center moves — just as the sun's sphere revolves around its center.

Every star has two motions: one is its own (dhātī) motion, and one is the secondary (qasr) motion, each differing from the other. The natural motion completes itself in the night and the daytime, revolving around its two centers, attributed to the great spheres within which the secondary motion operates. Thus the sphere of the sun revolves around its center from west to east, coming to the great circle — and this is what they call the Ecliptic (Falak al-Burūj). After this, by hypothetical assumption, a great circle whose center is the center of the universe, and whose two poles are the north and south poles, is found — and that circle is called the Celestial Equator (Mu'addal al-Nahār).

When we assume that the circle of the Ecliptic intersects the Celestial Equator, it divides it into two halves at two opposite points: one point is called the Vernal Equinox (I'tidāl Rabī'ī) and the other the Autumnal Equinox (I'tidāl Kharīfī).

After that, consider also the point of the equator (equinox) and the point of the ecliptic (falak al-buruj). If you take the two opposite points of it, one to the north and one to the south — for example, the point of the summer solstice and, to the south, the point of the winter solstice — then these two circles of the ecliptic divide it into two equal halves. The first quarter is that which lies between the vernal equinox point and the summer solstice point; this is called the season of spring, for as long as the sun travels that arc it is spring. And the arc between the summer solstice point and the autumnal equinox point is called the season of summer, for as long as the sun traverses that arc it is summer. The third quarter, between the autumnal equinox point and the winter solstice point, is called the season of autumn, for as long as the sun is on that arc it is autumn. And the fourth arc, between the winter solstice point and the vernal equinox point, is called the season of winter, for as long as the sun is on that arc it is winter.

After that, if we assume two great circles passing through the poles of the ecliptic and through the spring point and its opposite, the summer point, they divide it into four equal parts, producing the cardinal divisions. And when we extend these to six circles, each of which cuts the world at two opposite points along the ecliptic, each division is called a zodiacal sign (burj). If we then subdivide each sign, each sign contains thirty degrees, and the total of the six great circles together amounts to sixty parts. Once this is established and understood — as has been noted — it is well known that the fixed-star sphere (falak al-thawābit) is considered in two divisions, and in each division there are stars of various shapes and forms as described by the sages. Each division has a figure (sūra) and a configuration by which it is distinguished, as has been laid out. The meaning of the expression 'such-and-such a star is in such-and-such a zodiacal sign' is that a great circle drawn through…

The straight line is assumed to pass through the center of the ecliptic, striking [a point], separating [it], and the sphere comes to meet it at the first intersection. Ptolemy stated that every circular motion revolves around [the axis], completing eighty-six thousand [units], and seven hundred per mile for each motion of the ecliptic. It encompasses nine thousand [units], passing through three hundred [divisions].

Eighty-eight thousand and three hundred and ten miles in latitude, and a sixth of a degree per mile in width, one thousand [units] passing through three hundred, one hundred [units], and forty-two and a third miles. This is the Eleventh Perspective, which is the sphere that the religious scholars call the Throne ('Arsh), and astronomers call it the Encompassing Sphere (al-Falak al-A'zam). It surrounds all other spheres, and the greatest sphere is below all the other spheres.

The Atlas sphere (Falak al-Atlas) is below it — within it is a star of such magnitude — and the spheres move from east to west, opposite to the other spheres. The Atlas sphere moves along two opposite points: one toward the south pole and one toward the north pole, completing one revolution in a set period of hours. Its motion carries all the spheres and the stars in their motion.

Some have said this is because the greatest sphere is the container whose motion produces the observed movement, like a vessel carrying what is within it. This is what they have said, and the correct understanding is that the elements and the earth are encompassed within it — this is the proper explanation. The motion belongs to the bodies, not to the Exalted God. The greatest sphere has been given a force by which it moves, and the spheres within it are capable of moving anywhere — reaching near and far — and the greatest sphere moves. This motion, as the geometers have observed, is like the motion of the sun. That is to say, it is [a distance of] eight hundred farsakhs, and this is a proof of the correctness of the meaning, as shall be demonstrated.

It is reported and has come down to us: One day the Prophet, peace be upon them both, asked Gabriel about the time of prayer. Gabriel said: 'Do you not know? Come, I will show you.' On that day the sun had already traveled a distance of five hundred farsakhs in its movement. Rather, the sun performs its essential motion (al-haraka al-dhātiyya) from west to east, completing one full revolution around the greatest sphere (al-falak al-a'ẓam) in twenty-four hours, moving in its compelled motion (al-haraka al-qahriyya) from east to west. It turns from right to left, little by little, so that from left to right it proceeds as if gently, continuously, without ceasing, in opposition — and it is thus established that day and night arise from the motion of the greatest sphere. When the sun rises, as this sphere revolves, that side of the earth facing it is illuminated and brightened, and the living creatures there are moved toward it, and seeds sprout and plants grow and birds sing. But on the side away from it, as this sphere turns, the earth is dark and its air gloomy, and animals are still and plants dormant — until the sphere again moves and brings life back. The world continues in this orderly state of affairs. As the Almighty God, exalted and glorified, has said: 'And We have made the night a garment and the day for livelihood' (Qur'an 78:10-11). And in another place He says: 'And of His mercy He has made for you the night and the day, that you may rest therein, and that you may seek of His bounty, and that you may give thanks' (Qur'an 28:73). Most astronomers hold that beyond the greatest sphere there is nothing further — and this is a corrupt belief, for beyond it, they say, there is neither void nor plenum. As for the most eminent of the later scholars, Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad al-Razi, may God have mercy on him, he said: 'Whoever desires the kingdom of our sovereign intellect has exalted the prophets.' Muslim scholars have said: the Throne (kursī) is the sphere of the Law (falak al-nāmūs)...

The Throne (Arsh) is in the ninth sphere, and there is no doubt about its existence, for the verses and reports about it are without number and weight. He said in truth: 'His Throne extends over the heavens and the earth' (Quran 2:255), and 'He is the Lord of the Mighty Throne' (Quran 9:129). Abu al-Darr, may God be pleased with him, reported from the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, that he said: 'The seven heavens in relation to the Footstool (Kursi) are but like a ring thrown in a desert, and the superiority of the Throne over the Footstool is like the superiority of that desert over that ring.' That is, the Throne surpasses created things to such a degree that the Truth — Exalted and Majestic — made it the qibla of the people of spiritual stations, and it has been transmitted from Ja'far al-Sadiq, may God be pleased with him, that he said: There is no believer on earth who bows and prostrates himself but that his counterpart in the Throne also bows and prostrates, and the angels of that counterpart pray for that first believer and seek forgiveness for him. But when a believer on earth is occupied with sin and does not bow — at that moment the angels of that counterpart rebuke him until those believers are informed. The Messenger of God, peace be upon him, was asked about the speech: 'O You who reveal the mighty and conceal the ugly!' — and it is permissible for all creation whether seen or unseen to draw near to the Throne, though in truth its dimensions are such that the ninth sphere is but a limit beside it, and its depth no one but God the Exalted can measure. Its surface area is four hundred and seventy thousand and six hundred and sixty-two miles. The supreme sphere encompasses all the other spheres, and the spheres — some of them and others — and the terrestrial sphere together comprise thirteen spheres each encompassing the other. The most beautiful of forms is the spherical form, and for this reason the Exalted Truth — Glory and Majesty be His — created all things He mentioned and fashioned them in this form, as depicted here.

Verification of its station and precision of its aim: here in detail I wish to mention that this pure and generous thought — that the worlds of bodies should be encompassing — came about such that all bodies are divided into two divisions: one division is the simple bodies, which are the bodies of differing natures, and the other division is the compound bodies, that is to say, bodies of differing natures which are compounds. Among these are minerals, plants, and animals. One of the simples, which is a subdivision, consists of the elements — that is, earth, water, air, and fire — and another subdivision is the ethereal bodies together with the celestial spheres. The simple body, by its own nature and requirement, comes out spherical in form. The elements and ethereal bodies are spherical in shape, and it has come down that the earth likewise is capable of being spherical, though otherwise...

In that region (climate/zone), the arrangement of the stars is such that it resembles a desert plateau, and the mines appear in layers on the surface. The livelihoods of animals and humans depend upon it, and the springs of water flow there quickly, so that caravans draw water and it is as a vessel; and the material is not firmly fixed. Because when rising from the earth and ascending, one passes over the mountains and descends, moving and circling around.

And the concave (hollow) of its air — those same arrangements of the stars — completes a full circuit upon the earth, until it reaches that sphere of fire. All of the celestial spheres are encompassed within this form and arrangement, surrounding the earth entirely in its midst.

In the middle is the Earth; around it is the sphere of Water; around that is the sphere of Air; around that is the sphere of Fire; around that is the sphere of Mercury (Utarid); around that is the sphere of Venus (Zuhra); around that is the sphere of the Sun (Shams); around that is the sphere of Mars (Mirrikh); around that is the sphere of Jupiter (Mushtari); around that is the sphere of Saturn (Zuhal); around that is the sphere of the Fixed Stars; and beyond that is the outermost sphere, which appears beyond that circle, as has been mentioned.

From the detailed account mentioned above, it becomes clear that the stars rise from the East and set in the West — as is apparent. But the stars called 'Kanz' and the wandering ones face the spheres, not turning back, because the spheres are solid and not receptive to penetration or piercing. And since the simple spheres (al-aflak al-basita) are such, from them various effects proceed.

So it becomes known that the stars are embedded within the solid spheres, not floating freely within them, and the spheres encompass the Earth, surrounding it in their extent. The stars also extend in their lengths, and the movement of the spheres carries along the movement of the stars embedded within them — just as the movement of a millstone carries what is upon it. The stars are of two kinds: some are Planets (Sayyarat) and some are Fixed Stars (Thawaabit). The planets are seven, each moving upon its own sphere, level by level, and each of their movements produces effects.

The Twelfth Observation: Those who dwell in the heavens — all of them, without exception — are angels. An angel is a being endowed with life and rational speech, purified from the darkness of carnal impulses, passions, anger, and disobedience — things found, for example, among humans. God Most High has described them thus: 'They do not disobey God in what He commands them, but do what they are commanded.' They have no need of food or drink, they do not die, their nourishment is glorification and praise, their sanctification is exaltation, their rest is the remembrance of God Most High, and their joy is in worship. The creatures of the heavens differ in their forms and their ranks.

Know that the creation of angels was for the benefit and rectification of all created things. That angels exist in the celestial spheres is established; it is also confirmed by rational proof, for God Most High did not leave the spheres disordered and empty. Rather, He created within them various kinds of living beings, filled the air with birds, the dry land with beasts and wild animals, the mountains with solid creatures, and populated the darkness and dust — indeed, He created kinds of living beings and filled them with souls to overflowing, and for every spring, valley, and mine there are angels appointed. How then could the luminous, transparent spheres — the most refined of all God Most High's creations — be empty of angels?

The angels are of all kinds, and God Most High alone knows their true number, as He said: 'And none knows the hosts of your Lord except Him.' It is reported from the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, in a well-known tradition that from the atoms of the universe there is not a single space the size of a hand's span but an angel is appointed over it. Not a single drop of rain descends without an angel being assigned to it. And upon the Throne and the Footstool, there is no spot, however small, that is not occupied by an angel engaged in worship — as is well established.

The Messenger of God — upon whom be the finest of blessings — declared: 'The most pleasant of fragrances and the truest of rights belong to…' Upon that place, this span [of heaven] exists, and upon it the angels are prostrate. The angels — not one type but of many kinds — serve [God] and draw apart from it. The Creator of the universe has described them from within [His knowledge], saying: 'We have no station save a known one, and verily we are ranged in ranks, and verily we give glory [to God].' It follows that some angels perform the prayer as Adam's community does, standing in straight rows, upright in posture, remaining standing in prayer before God.

And some angels are in a state of bowing (rukū') in their worship, never disdaining [to serve]. As the Lord of Glory declares: 'Those who are in His presence do not disdain to worship Him' — by this is meant the honor of nearness [to God].

Some angels are in prostration, and within [the context of] prostration it is permissible — indeed, in that state [it is required] — as the Word of God Most High is proof of this: 'And when We said to the angels: Prostrate yourselves before Adam, so they prostrated, except Iblis — he refused and was arrogant and was of the disbelievers' [Quran 2:34]. But from this standalone argument, what is meant is the shari'a meaning, and by 'angels' is meant all of them — that is, this is to be understood in that manner.

And some angels are seated, continuously engaged in praise and glorification — they are the angels of praise (hamd).

Story: Uwais al-Qarani — may God have mercy on him — is reported to have said: 'I shall worship in such a way that the angels in heaven will take note.' One night he would stand [in prayer] from the beginning until dawn, and another night he would remain in bowing (ruku') from the beginning until dawn, and another night he would remain in prostration (sujud) from the beginning until dawn.
The first night he would prostrate from dawn onward, spending the night entirely in worship.

And know that angels are pure spiritual essences, different in nature from rational souls, truly distinct, and devoted entirely [to God]. Some are assigned to ranks of immersion [in divine worship], and recitation is their glorification, and they are called the noble ones — 'They glorify [God] night and day without ceasing' [Quran 21:20]. They are arranged in the ranks of the highest angels. And one group is turned away [from created things], and their recitation is eternal in the primordial [realm], and they act and move, and some of them are: 'Those who pull out forcefully, those who draw out gently, those who glide [through the heavens], those who race ahead, and those who direct affairs [by God's command]' [Quran 79:1-5].
The angels of the [divine] retinue — each one of them has numerous wings and feathers, as it is reported that around the Throne of God — Mighty and Exalted be His remembrance — [they gather in forms].

God made the angels as messengers with wings, two, three, and four — arranged in ranks of blessed candles.
Among them are those assigned to the heavens and some to the earth, among whom are the prophets, peace be upon them, and the earthly angels.
There is debate as to which is superior — the earthly angels or the heavenly angels.
Some of the angels have the forms of horses and buraq-like shapes, and these are the ones described here, for the Creator fashioned them.
In this elevated station, He gave them beautiful forms — and God is the best of creators.

The caption text between the two illustrations reads:
'All the angels together — the angels of the Throne — stand around [the Throne] ceaselessly, shaped without form. They continually intercede on behalf of the children of Adam, seek out their provisions, and pray to the Divine Presence [on their behalf].'

The marginal text (a continuation or commentary passage in a different hand) elaborates on the same theme: discussing the angels who, among all angelic beings, have attained the highest excellence — namely the angels of the Throne (ʿArsh), who stand perpetually in service, interceding for the children of Adam, seeking their sustenance, and supplicating before God Almighty on their behalf. The passage closes with what appear to be scribal notations or ownership marks: Saʿīd, Waṣṣāf, Muntaẓir.

The lower illustration shows a solitary white-bearded figure (likely Adam) kneeling in supplication, with water or light surrounding him, consistent with the text's theme of Adam's children being prayed over by the angels.

And one [angel] is in the form of an ox, constantly praying for the sake of livestock and seeking their provision.

And one [angel] is in the form of a lion, constantly praying for the sake of predatory animals and seeking their provision.

And one [angel] is in the form of a vulture, constantly praying for the sake of birds and seeking their provision.

God Most High has said: 'They do not grow weary of glorifying their Lord, nor do they tire' — meaning that on the Day of Resurrection, the angels carrying the Throne and the angels close to God seek forgiveness on behalf of the believers before God Most High. This refers to the verse: 'Those who carry the Throne and those surrounding it glorify the praise of their Lord, believe in Him, and seek forgiveness for those who believe: Our Lord, You encompass all things in mercy.' The angels form rows — one group you see as a single angel in one row, and all other angels form another row — as in the verse: 'The Day when the Spirit and the angels stand in rows.' Some commentators have explained this by saying that 'the Spirit' (Ruh) here means a specific angel, because from his single breath life is generated. He is the angel appointed over the celestial spheres, set in motion over Mecca and the heavens and the elements and minerals and plants and animals. He is the most powerful, greatest, and noblest of the angels in the corporeal realm, the highest among material beings. Just as he is able to keep the spheres stationary or set them in motion, some scholars have said: 'If the heavens and the earth were commanded to glorify God, they would.' It is related from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with him, that this angel has a face toward the west and a face toward the east, and between his two eyes are a thousand paths, and in each path are a thousand lights. With a single utterance of glorification he praises God Most High, and whoever hears his voice would be so overwhelmed that all creatures would perish. When the angels finish their glorification and praise, all of them together would not equal even one of his glorifications. And it is said he has glorified God a thousand times and more.

And you, the angel of the Trusted Spirit (Israfil) enters the layers of the earth and its depths, and his measured power pervades everything, and he is one of the great angels. Israfil is the one who carries the souls and delivers them to their bodies. His form fills the distance between heaven and earth, and the trumpet (Sur) has hollows like channels, and in each channel there are fifty thousand souls that have entered it. Israfil has his trumpet ready, and he gazes toward the Throne, waiting — as soon as he is commanded to blow, he stands ready. He will blow it three times: the first blast will terrify all who dwell in the heavens and on the earth, as the Creator of the universe has said: 'And the Day the Trumpet is blown — and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will be terrified, except whom Allah wills.' With the second blast, all creation will die, as He has said: 'And the Trumpet will be blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will fall dead, except whom Allah wills.' And with the third blast, all souls will be gathered together, as the verse following the second announces: 'Then it will be blown again, and at once they will be standing, looking on.' Israfil has four wings: one toward the east, one toward the west, one spread below toward the earth to walk upon, and one covering his face — he has covered himself out of awe of the Most High. He stands beneath the Throne, and his words reach the farthest point. The Preserved Tablet (Lawh Mahfuz) is like a spiritual garden within him, wherein the Most High creates things. The Pen, by divine command, records upon the Preserved Tablet — Israfil receives that command and transmits it. He alone sees it and delivers it; he has among the angels certain assistants who carry out the blowing and the bestowal of the power of life upon animals, plants, minerals, and all the angels, one of whom...

Gabriel — he is called the Trustee of Revelation, the Guardian of the Holy, and the Faithful Spirit. It is in this regard that God Most High has said: 'The Faithful Spirit descended with it upon your heart.' He is also called the Holy Spirit, and the Greatest Peacock, and the Peacock of the Angels. God Most High revealed to His presence one hundred and four scriptures in total: ten pages upon Adam, peace be upon him; and thirty pages upon Seth, peace be upon him; and thirty pages upon Idris, peace be upon him; and ten pages upon Abraham, peace be upon him; and the Torah upon Moses, peace be upon him; and the Psalms upon David, peace be upon him; and the Gospel upon Jesus, peace be upon him; and the Quran upon the Seal of the Prophets, Muhammad the Chosen One, may God's blessings and peace be upon him. Concerning Gabriel, God Most High says: 'One possessed of power, secure in the presence of the Lord of the Throne.' His power is such that he lifted six towns of the people of Lot from the depths of the earth and raised them close to the sky, so near that the angels could hear the crowing of their roosters and the barking of their dogs, and then he struck them from above so that rays descended upon them. And consider the full measure of that power — he went to Abraham, peace be upon him, in his dwelling, and in that very moment the Honored One Gabriel descended from his station swiftly by the road of the spring to Abraham and descended from on high. And Joseph, peace be upon him — his brothers threw him into the pit, and immediately God Most High sent Gabriel down from his lofty station. Gabriel descended at once and Joseph, peace be upon him, was cast into the well, and he guided him and made him steadfast, and Moses was before Pharaoh — at that very moment he came swiftly and in an instant delivered Moses, and such is the might of his power.

It becomes known that this person, Bölük Bey, was killed, and the Divine decree had certainly established this rank.

It is such that the other angels became completely silent upon this, two of them standing firm in their places, reporting what happened. When God the Exalted sends revelation through the sound of a chain striking, the angels of death receive it. Gabriel came to them and said that one had fainted. Upon questioning Gabriel about what had occurred, the others argued about the rank, and Gabriel said that those angels, whose wings were in proper station, were responsible for guarding their stations.

Those mighty angels, because of their service and functions assigned to them, are charged with guarding the world — to repel evil and bring good to humans and all other creatures, and this has always been so. The Messenger of God, peace be upon him, said to Gabriel, peace be upon him: 'I wish to see you as you truly are — show me your true form.' So Gabriel showed himself on the Night of Power (Laylat al-Qadr), that is, on a night when the moon was full. The Messenger of God stood there amazed at what he saw. He saw Gabriel filling the entire horizon. The Messenger of God was struck with awe and nearly lost consciousness. Then he recovered and saw Gabriel had returned to his familiar form.

Know that God the Exalted has created none among His creation comparable to Gabriel — Israfil stands to his right, and he passes through the night below the Throne, at times near the highest heaven and at times near the earth below, traveling with great speed.

Among all the angels, one of the greatest is Mikail, who is charged with overseeing the sustenance (rizq) of all creation, keeping account of it, and is also responsible for knowledge and wisdom. He oversees souls, for life depends on nourishment from God. He is stationed between heaven and earth, and Mikail's place is described as being in the gathering place (Mahshar), and his final end...

And the governors and rulers among the angels — their number is known only to God Almighty. If all the dead were to open [their records], even a person of sound mind could not count them. If one of them were to manifest their glory, the light from which they are made would be blinding, and their helpers who descend therein would be of a power and strength beyond [reckoning].

HIKAYA (Story): One day Umar, may God be pleased with him, was teaching some Jews, and Jibrīl (Gabriel) was asked about it. One of the Jews said: 'You have informed us of our secrets and unveiled our mysteries — and that guest is a punishment from the angel Mālik and Mīkā'īl (Michael).' They spoke of their enmity and hostility, and Umar, may God be pleased with him, said: 'What then is their station with God Almighty?' They replied: 'Jibrīl is on the right side and Mīkā'īl on the left side, and between the two of them there is enmity.' Umar, may God be pleased with him, said: 'What you have said is not so — for they are your enemies and adversaries.' And he said to the unbelievers: 'You are more unbelieving than anyone.' While Umar, may God be pleased with him, was in the presence of the Messenger of God, this noble verse was revealed:

'Whoever is an enemy to God and His angels and His messengers and Jibrīl and Mīkā'īl — then indeed God is an enemy to the disbelievers.' [Quran 2:98]

Among all the angels, 'Izrā'īl (the Angel of Death) and Abū Barr are the angels appointed over every place of settlement and over the seizing of souls. His station is in the highest heaven, and his feet are at the lowest earth, and his face is turned toward the Preserved Tablet (Lawḥ al-Maḥfūẓ), and all the earth is under his gaze. No one can be compared to him in any way. It is said that no one else is able to take a soul from any place — 'Izrā'īl knows from where, and goes and seizes it. And from the Preserved Tablet he knows the appointed time of every person, and when the time comes he seizes the soul either in person or through his helpers.

HIKAYA: Ibrāhīm [Abraham] said to 'Izrā'īl: 'If someone is in the East and [another in the West]...

And for every person whose appointed time (ajal) has come in the west, and plague has struck one land, and famine has struck another land — I dispatch the souls, for the Most High God has commanded me, saying: Come and take them. The angels who are subordinate to me are present, and they seize them together. This is the meaning of the verse: 'Until when death comes to one of you, Our messengers take him, and they do not fall short' (Quran 6:61). By 'messengers' is meant Azra'il and his assistants.

A Story: Solomon (peace be upon him) said that he wished to see Azra'il in his true form. Suddenly Azra'il appeared before Solomon, and Solomon was frightened. Azra'il said: 'O Lord, grant Solomon strength so that he may look upon me.' Revelation came: 'Let Solomon gaze upon him.' Then Solomon stood firm, and Azra'il appeared to Solomon in his true form. Solomon said to Azra'il: 'How many kings are under you?' Azra'il replied: 'One foot of mine is more than a king's domain in vastness, and from beneath my feet there are more rays of light than above my head, and now the awe of it has overwhelmed the servants. Those who see me — I seize their souls at the moment I appear to them.'

A Story: On a Tuesday, Azra'il came to visit Solomon (peace be upon him). Solomon asked him: 'Why do you not give respite to people and allow them time? How does it feel when a soul departs, and how does it feel when souls meet their end, and how does it feel when you come to seize a soul?' Azra'il replied: 'In the month of Sha'ban a list arrives for me containing the names of thousands upon thousands of people whose souls are to be taken. The list of their names is written, and among them are some whose souls I am to seize in that period — either by direct dispatch or through the Preserved Tablet (Lawh al-Mahfuz). But as for whether the souls of those who professed the unity of God (tawhid) are in a state of well-being — yes, they are.'

He seized it and threw the cloak over his upper part, pressing it down, saying 'O people of the Turks, prayers be upon God's Messenger.' He seized it and dipped it in pitch, pressing it against the lower part, saying 'truly and certainly.' — A Story —

It is narrated that Azrael came to the presence of Solomon, peace be upon him, and was present at his assembly. Azrael fixed his gaze intently upon a certain man. When Azrael departed, that man said — meaning he asked — 'Why did Azrael look at me so much?' Solomon said: 'Azrael looked at you excessively; if you fear, go to the farthest lands of India.' So he went there. Afterward, Azrael returned to Solomon, peace be upon him, and Solomon said to him: 'You stared intently at one of my attendants; why did you fix your gaze on him with such concentration?' Azrael said: 'I was commanded to take his soul there near you, and when I saw him standing before me I was astonished. Then at that very moment I went and took his soul.' — A Story concerning Azrael and David, peace be upon him —

Two men came to David with a dispute. David asked Azrael about how many days remained of one man's life. After some time had passed, that man recovered his health. David then asked Azrael about this. Azrael replied: 'That righteous poor man gave charity, and God Most High accepted it from him, for He has said: Charity wards off calamity and increases lifespan.' So it became apparent according to the verse: 'God erases what He wills and confirms what He wills, and with Him is the Mother of the Book.' This was combined with the blessing of that prayer. God's mercy: this verse has two interpretations — one is that the apparent outward meaning shows that in that land each person has one allotted provision, fortune and misfortune, sustenance and life — and the other is that those who are chosen differ from some things outwardly and from the angels in some ways that are hidden.

These are the angels who are mentioned as the Muqarrabun (those brought near to God). These are described in books as being in the Divine Presence, their every inclination toward anything other than God Almighty being recorded. Among the angels of the heavens, the angels of the first sphere appear in the form of a bull; the angels of the second sphere in the form of an eagle; the angels of the third sphere in the form of a rooster; the angels of the fourth sphere in the form of a horse; the angels of the fifth sphere in the form of a hoopoe bird; the angels of the sixth sphere in the form of a lynx; and the angels of the seventh sphere appear in human form. Beyond the seventh sphere there are angels, some of whom converse with one another in different languages praising God with various glorifications. Among the angels there are some called the Noble Recorders (Kiram al-Katibin). God Almighty has also appointed guardians over these, as He said: 'And verily over you are guardians, noble recorders, who know whatever you do.' God Almighty has described them thus: they are 'guardians' because they record and preserve all the deeds of His servants; they are described as 'noble' because they are honored in the sight of God Almighty, since they strive in obedience to Him; they are described as 'recorders' because they write down the deeds of servants. They are also described as having knowledge of all the actions of servants — not by conjecture, but with certainty. Their knowledge encompasses in particular the outward deeds of the limbs, and also the inner deeds of the hearts — the good intentions they recognize by a pleasant fragrance, and the evil intentions by a foul odor. As for these guardian angels, some say there are two for each person — one on the right who records good deeds and one on the left who records evil deeds, with the angel on the right being the supervisor over the one on the left. Others say there are four: two for the day and two for the night. And for each person there is yet another angel who serves as a protector.

Those angels who are present when a believer departs from this world, until the Almighty commands them, 'Remain near the grave and continue reciting glorification and praise until the Day of Resurrection.' Among the angels are those called the Muaqqibat, who descend with blessings, and souls and deeds ascend to God through them. Among the angels are Munkar and Nakir, who are dark-colored angels that enter the grave and question the deceased within it. Among the angels are those called the Mustarahun, who are permitted to gather in the assemblies of those engaged in remembrance of God and righteous worship. Among the angels are Harut and Marut, whose story is well known: they were pious angels who criticized humanity, asking God why Adam's progeny were susceptible to passion, forgetfulness, and the temptation of Satan. To refute their argument and to put them to the test, God Most High caused Harut and Marut to be given human form and human nature. A woman named Zuhrah was sent to tempt them and to arouse their desire. She excited and provoked them with passion. Afterward, Zuhrah sought a way to ascend to the heavens. The angels then realized the severity of the punishment that awaited them. They sought the intercession of Idris, peace be upon him, who was alive at that time, mentioning their story before him and asking him to pray on their behalf. God Most High gave them the choice between the punishment of this world and the punishment of the hereafter, and the choice was made lawful. They chose the punishment of this world, and in Babylon they were placed in chains as a restraint and will remain punished until the Day of Resurrection. This is the story. According to some commentators, the words of God Most High — 'And what was sent down upon the two angels in Babylon, Harut and Marut' — are interpreted in this manner. However, the scholars of true investigation among the commentators have not accepted this interpretation. Among the angels are those appointed as guardians over creation and its correction, and some angels among them have been assigned by God Most High to ward off corruption.

For example, food may be rice, or something even more excellent — when a person eats it, a reward comes to him from the angels. One angel attracts the nutrients of food to the flesh and bones, for food causes movement within the self. Another angel of regret comes to ensure that the innate heat performs its function. Another angel gives form to the blood and refines it. Another angel manages the waste products, distributing them. Another angel separates the flesh, bones, and sinews from one another. Another angel is assigned to take on the form of the bones and the form of the flesh, while another angel oversees the proportions, ensuring nothing exceeds its proper measure. Each organ has its own angel and its own house, ensuring that what is hollow remains hollow and what is solid remains solid, so that the food appropriate to a given organ matches its shape and form — if it does not match, it becomes altered and takes on a more unpleasant form. The fine and transparent part of food goes to the eyes and the pure part stays there, while the thick part goes to the bones and connects them. It takes on the appropriate shape and form for each organ. Some portions go to certain organs, and some go to others, distributed by weight, and some organs grow large — thus the management of the whole body proceeds. All of these angels are appointed as overseers and are constantly engaged in the administration of the body; not one of them is idle at any moment. This is how it is with all created things: not one exists without a great angel or several angels appointed over it.

The Thirteenth Consideration: Concerning Time. There are several positions on this matter. First, what is the true nature of time? There are many schools of thought among the philosophers. Some ancient sages held that time is simply continuous motion. One view is that time is the self-motion of the greatest celestial sphere. A strange view holds that time is the revolution of the greatest sphere. Another view holds that time is the measure of the motion of the greatest sphere. Yet another view holds that time is something renewed. What is well known is that these views are successive and renewed in an indefinite way — for example, when one says 'Zayd came at such-and-such a time,' one understands it as...

At the time it rises, according to the well-known position of those who hold that the discourse happens at the time of sunrise — the opinion preferred by the scholars of astronomy — the duration of the motion of the greatest celestial sphere is understood, that is to say, the time is divided into epochs, and epochs are divided into years, and years are divided into months, and months are divided into weeks, and weeks are divided into days and nights, and days and nights are divided into hours, and hours are divided into moments. Time is the capital of a human being, from which happiness is earned.

Verse (bayt): This is the counsel, O dear one — your life is precious, do not waste it. That is to say, time dissolves like glass, passing away quickly. Observe this: little time remains while much has gone.

Your age passes, and your lifespan goes on unknown to you, though it is known to God. Like a traveler, life moves swiftly, cutting through its stages continuously; you have no rest for even a moment along its way. Each day brings one station, every hour a league, every moment a mile. With each breath one draws, that breath departs toward its end. Ninety-some cycles pass — that is to say, the months — as God Most High has said: "Indeed, the number of months with God is twelve months in the Book of God from the day He created the heavens and the earth; of these, four are sacred" (Qur'an 9:36). The Arabs used to say a year is three hundred sixty-four days, and the months of those who are attached to what is above the crescent — the period between them — are called the intercalary days (ayyam al-nasi'). Whether day or night passes, those who claim that celestial configurations cause events are always complaining against the celestial spheres.

Poem (shi'r): What fault have the arrows coming from where I cannot see? And how can I be safe from an archer while the archer is not visible?

The order of the Muhammadan law becomes established, and the accidents of divine decree and the determination of God Most High become known. Attribution of events to other than God is forbidden, as the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, said: 'Do not liken anything to God.' God alone is the Creator, the One who arranges and manages all affairs. He is the Lord — good and evil, fortune and misfortune, joy and sorrow all return to Him. Every thread is woven by His hand.

Second Chapter: On the days of the year — specifically the Day of Arafah — from the rising of the sun to its setting, and in religious law, the period between the break of dawn and the setting of the sun is called 'day,' and the period between sunset and the next sunrise is called 'night.' The night and day together, reckoned as four watches, complete the full revolution of the celestial sphere. God Most High says in this regard: 'He causes the night to enter into the day, and He causes the day to enter into the night.' Each time one grows longer, the other grows shorter. The lengths of night and day vary: sometimes the day is extremely short — perhaps only six hours — and sometimes it is seven hours, and the night reaches its maximum length and the day its minimum in the month of Kanun al-Awwal (December), when the sun enters Capricorn. From that point onward the day begins to lengthen and the night to shorten, until in the month of Haziran (June), when the sun reaches the end of Gemini, the day and night become equal — each being twelve hours. This is the autumnal equinox. From that point the night grows longer and the day shorter, reaching the maximum length of night and minimum length of day in Kanun al-Awwal again, when the process reverses: the night shortens and the day lengthens, continuing until Adhar (March).

...on the fifteenth day, because the sun comes to its end overnight, and day and night become equal — that is twelve hours each — this is the time when day and night are equal until the Book of God makes clear: 'And the sun runs to its resting place; that is the decree of the Mighty, the All-Knowing.' Indeed, every night and day, the seasons of the year — the four seasons mentioned — the spring being half of the summer... the eighth prayer according to one view, in the shortest time, which is when day and night are equal, that is when it becomes narrow and precise. And day and night are set for the movement and livelihood of mankind, and its movement is determined like that of a city dweller. Thus the Almighty and His family and the scholars determined one fixed time in daylight for movement and one fixed time in the night for rest, so that if it were not so, the affairs of mankind would be wasted and ruined in their lifetimes.

The Third Section: On the virtues of the days and the special properties of the months. Since the day of Friday has been honored, let us begin with it:

Friday — this day is called 'Jum'a' (Friday/Gathering) because it is the day of gathering for prayer, when the Almighty, having finished creating the worlds, gathered all creation together. And Friday is the day of the Hanafi community, and it is recorded as the festival of the believers and the pillar of places, and it is a blessed day for worship and the seeking of one's needs. It is a day of union and visitation, a day of marriage — just as Adam married [Eve], and Solomon married the Queen of Sheba, and Joseph married Zulaykha, and Moses married Saffura, and Fatima of the Prophets — the Chosen One, peace and blessings of God be upon him — [married] Khadija, and [later] Aisha...

It was on Friday that the marriage took place, and Adam, peace be upon him, was created on Friday — that is, his soul was breathed into him on Friday — and he entered Paradise on a Friday, and he was taken out of Paradise on a Friday, and his repentance was accepted on a Friday, and his soul was taken on a Friday, and the Trumpet will be blown on a Friday, and the Resurrection...

Repentance: The Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, said that there is no day that the sun rises upon more virtuous than Friday, and whoever arrives at the right time on Friday, their prayer is certainly answered. And it is reported that whoever dies on a Friday night or during the day of Friday, they will most likely be buried free from the punishment of the grave. Whoever cuts their nails on Friday will be safe from poverty — though some say they will become wealthy. 

A Story: Al-Asma'i said: The Commander of the Faithful Harun al-Rashid looked at me on a Friday and said: 'I see you cutting your nails.' He said: 'O Asma'i, cutting nails on Friday is a Sunnah and drives away poverty.' I said: 'O Commander of the Faithful, do you fear poverty?' He replied: 'Who among those under my sovereignty does not fear it?'

And it is a blameworthy innovation that a traveler departs on Friday morning, for it was the custom at the beginning of Islam that people would come to the mosque for the dawn prayer and remain there until they had performed the Friday prayer, and it is reported that it was thus established. Whoever regularly attends the Friday prayer, God lightens [his burden] for him and the angels of the highest realm pray for him. If he comes for the sake of the poor, then O heedless one! And if he comes for the sake of religion, let him fulfill it. If he comes for the sake of his health, let him seek remedy — for each one of these intentions has its merit.

As for the day of Saturday: The word 'Sabt' (Saturday) is a verbal noun meaning veneration and cessation of activity — the Jews observed it in veneration, and thus it was called Sabt, for on that day time ceased [for them] and came to a halt. It is also said that Sabt comes from 'resting' (istirāḥa). The Jews became very numerous on account of this day, which is why this day is called the day of the Jews and the day of cunning, because deceit spread among them and trickery became their trait.

God says that He planned a great scheme, and God Most High says it regarding Joseph, peace be upon him, when his brothers schemed against him: God Most High says 'What you did to Joseph.' Regarding Salih, when those of his people schemed against the she-camel which was a trial for them, God Almighty says: 'And they schemed and We schemed, while they did not perceive.' Regarding Moses, when his people schemed with magic and sorcery against him, God Most High says: 'So devise your scheme, then come in ranks.' Regarding when the Jews called him a sorcerer and plotted against him, God Most High says: 'And they schemed and God schemed, and God is the best of schemers.' Regarding the Seal of the Prophets, the noble Mustafa, peace and blessings of God be upon him, when the chieftains of Quraysh gathered in the Dar al-Nadwa to plot against him, God Most High says: 'And when those who disbelieved plotted against you to imprison you, or kill you.' On the Sabbath day, near the trunk of a date palm tree, they came to seize him on the Sabbath, but he eluded them and escaped. Moses, by the command of God Most High, told the Children of Israel that each week one day should be set aside free from worldly occupations. They chose the Sabbath for this devotion, so as to be free from worldly preoccupations, turning their hearts wholly to God. But on that very day fish appeared in abundance; on other days no fish came. This was a test. They said: 'On the Sabbath, we shall not work nor engage in trade and commerce, and there is no harm in carrying burdens.' But it is said that the Jews, in contravention of this, used that day for labor, and they considered it blessed. The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, said: 'This speech of mine you must memorize and preserve.'

Saturday and Thursday: It is said that Saturday fishing is especially blessed. Sunday is the first day of this world: God Almighty began the creation of the world [on Sunday] and completed it on Friday, for it is said 'Your Lord is God, who created the heavens and the earth in six days.' Planting gardens and orchards and building [structures] was begun [on Sunday]. Abu Dharr al-Ghifari, may God be pleased with him, said: The Messenger of God, peace be upon him, was asked about Sunday and he said: 'It is a day of planting and building.' When asked why, he replied: 'Because on it the world and its cultivation were begun.' God Almighty, from His own names, chose two names for [Sunday]: one of them is 'Ahad' [One], so that none would be equal to it; and the second naming [Ahad] was given because that day was the beginning of creation, and 'Wahid' was assigned to it because it signifies the Singular. God Almighty named it thus for purposes of distinction. It is said that Sunday is auspicious for beginning journeys.

Monday: It is a blessed day, as the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, said: 'On this day I was born, on this day Gabriel brought revelation to me, on this day I emigrated from Mecca to Medina, and on this day my soul departed.' The deeds of servants are presented [to God] on Mondays and Thursdays. This is why the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, used to fast on Mondays, saying: 'It is a day on which deeds are raised up, and I wish my deeds to be raised while I am fasting.' On this day Abraham the Prophet laid the foundations of the Kaaba and offered his prayers. On this day prayers ascend [to heaven]. Anas ibn Malik, may God be pleased with him, related that the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, said regarding Monday: 'It is a day of travel and answered prayers.' When asked why, O Messenger of God, he said: I cannot describe it [fully]...

On commerce and profit in trade: Ahmad ibn Hanbal ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with him, reported this. On Tuesday, the creatures of the mountains and animals are superior. In the town of Darqan, the twin marks [appear] and the remedy is indicated. On that day, the creature saw something, and Qabil killed someone from the sons of Malik, may God be pleased with him. [Story:] Hamrun ibn Ismail said: One day I came to the Caliph al-Mu'tasim and he related to me — on the authority of Rashid, from Mahdi, from Mansur, from his father, from his grandfather, from Ibn 'Abkal — that the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, was asked: 'Whoever undergoes cupping on Thursday in those days of the month' — meaning whoever among us undergoes cupping — 'and if he falls ill, he will recover from that illness. Now let us explain the names of the hours of the day and night from memory. The time called 'fajr' (dawn) — after it comes 'sabah' (morning) — after it comes 'ghada' (early morning meal time) — after it comes 'bukra' (early morning) — after it comes 'duha' (forenoon) — after it comes 'dakhw' — after it comes 'hajira' (midday heat) — after it comes 'zuhr' (noon) — after it comes 'rawah' (mid-afternoon) — after it comes 'asr' (afternoon prayer time) — after it comes 'asr' — after it comes 'isha al-ula' (early evening) — after it comes 'isha al-akhira' (late evening). Now for the hours of the night: if one wishes to know them, they are enumerated here. One who travels by foot from that point onward, moving through them in order, will come to know them.

And the fifth [matter]: the excellence of Ashura has been reported in hadiths, [as has] the month of Rabi al-Awwal, which is the month of the Prophet's birth, peace and blessings of God be upon him, and Rajab. The first of the month of Muharram, and half of Sha'ban on its fifteenth, and of Ramadan on its fourteenth, and some say its first, some say its revelation night, some say its ninth — and Eid al-Fitr and the days of the well-known [pilgrimage], that is, from the nineteenth of Dhu al-Hijja, which is Eid al-Adha, and Eid al-Adha. And Mondays, Thursdays, and Fridays are noble nights; their noble nights are: the eve of Ashura, the eve of the first of Rajab, the eve of mid-[Sha'ban], and some say the eves of Ramadan on its fourteenth, fifteenth, and seventeenth, and the eve of Eid al-Fitr, and the eve of Eid al-Adha. On these noble days and excellent nights, one should refrain from sins and seek acts of worship and fulfillment of needs; these are auspicious seasons. As for the four seasons, they are known by the peoples of all nations — Arabs, Romans, Persians, Copts, Turks, Indians, Zanj, and others — though they differ in their months and their reckonings. The Arab, Roman, and Persian months are the most concise. The Arab month begins with the sighting of the new crescent moon, and the number of its days varies — sometimes twenty-nine, sometimes thirty. This is the nature of the Arab months. As for the others, they follow fixed reckonings of twenty-nine or thirty days. God Almighty has said: 'Indeed, the number of months with God is twelve months in the Book of God, [decreed] the day He created the heavens and the earth; of these, four are sacred.' These are: Rajab, which stands alone, and Dhu al-Qa'da, Dhu al-Hijja, and Muharram — these are the sacred months. Their added sanctity means that in them, obedience to God brings greater reward, and sin brings greater punishment.

Concerning the sacred months: In these months the law of Abraham and Ishmael holds, and in these months it is the tradition of the Arabs to establish justice and equity, and in particular to abandon fighting and set aside grievances. In these months, whoever had a dispute or complaint with another would reconcile and make peace. It has been mentioned that the details thereof make clear that some Arabs follow the lunar calendar and some the solar calendar. The solar year is three hundred and sixty-five days, and the difference between the two is that the sun completes its orbit; and God Most High said: 'And they stayed in their cave three hundred years and added nine' (Quran 18:25). That is, the People of the Cave remained in that cave for three hundred years plus nine, and this difference is that of the solar year. It is well-known among the Arabs and counted thus:

Muharram 30 days, Safar 29, Rabi' al-Awwal 30, Rabi' al-Akhir 29, Jumada al-Ula 30, Jumada al-Akhira 29, Rajab [30], Sha'ban 29, Ramadan [30], Shawwal 29, Dhu al-Qa'da 30, Dhu al-Hijja 29.

Having set forth the above, let it be known that Muharram is a blessed month. It is called Muharram because the kings forbade [fighting in it]. Some say that in it there is a particular virtue and benefit. It is said that at its beginning the Arabs would cease their conflicts and disputes, and Jonah (Yunus), son of Amittai, emerged from the belly of the fish on a certain day thereof — some say it was the fourteenth day. It is said that the Throne, the Footstool (Arsh), Paradise, Michael, Israfil, and Gabriel were all created on a day within it. The ascension of Idris took place on a day in it, and the angel Malik [guardian of Hell] was created on it. On the tenth day, which is Ashura, it is incumbent upon all nations to venerate it, for on it the repentance of Adam was accepted.

STORY of Abdullah ibn Bajis:

The Commander of the Faithful, Umar (may God be pleased with him), once saw among the people a man who was blind and lame, and this person was barely able to manage with a little assistance. Umar (may God be pleased with him) said: 'I witnessed a most terrible sight.' One of those present in that assembly said: 'What do you make of him, O Commander of the Faithful?' Umar (may God be pleased with him) said: 'That person said: He is Abu Arj of Sana'a, [named] Salma. He directed a curse-prayer against me and I became thus.' Umar ordered Iyad to be brought. When he came, Umar (may God be pleased with him) said: 'Tell me the news of this son of Sana'a and his condition.' Iyad said: 'In the time of [pre-Islamic] ignorance, he would speak, then when Islam came, Umar (may God be pleased with him) dismissed it.' Then he narrated to him the story plainly. Iyad said: 'O Commander of the Faithful, this man of Sana'a had ten daughters from [his wife] Sana'a, and of those ten daughters, one died. Then this man of Sana'a took all wealth from me unjustly, and despite all my explanations it was of no use. I endured with patience until finally this person came, and I was moved to make this supplication: O God, I call upon You earnestly—favor me over the people of Sana'a, strike down this man—but it was of no avail to me.' Then nine [afflictions] fell upon him one by one, and he was rendered unable to move or stir, and grateful was he. When Umar (may God be pleased with him) heard this, he said: 'Glory be to God, this is a wondrous matter!' The Messenger of God, peace be upon him, showed this to the people of his household and narrated it story by story, and on that day Gabriel came and conveyed the revelation. On the eighteenth day of this month, Gabriel came to him and called it the great one, and this month is called Ramadan — it is called Ramadan because at the time when the heat of Ramadan endures and is felt intensely, it is harmful and the shade of the sun's rays comes. Fifth Chapter: Concerning the Roman (Rum) calendar — the calendar of Rum (Anatolia/Byzantium), which is the calendar accepted among the Romans, established by Alexander son of Philip the Macedonian. According to it, the solar year consists of three hundred and sixty-five days, and every four years one additional day is added, making three hundred and sixty-six days, and that year is called a leap year (kabise). The year is divided into months, which are as follows:
March (Ādhār) • April (Nīsān) • May (Ayyār) • June (Ḥazīrān) • July (Tammūz) • August (Āb) • September (Aylūl) • October (Tishrīn al-Awwal) • November (Tishrīn al-Thānī) • December (Kānūn al-Awwal) • January (Kānūn al-Thānī) • February (Shubāṭ).
Of these, four months — Tishrīn al-Thānī, Nīsān, Ḥazīrān, and Aylūl — have thirty days each. Seven months — Tishrīn al-Awwal, Kānūn al-Awwal, Kānūn al-Thānī, Ādhār, Ayyār, Āb, and Tammūz — have thirty-one days each. And February (Shubāṭ) has twenty-eight days and a quarter, so that in every fourth year one full day is added, making it a leap year. As for the Falak (celestial sphere), the months of the Romans differ in number because the solar year being the basis, and the sun's motion through the signs being unequal, the lengths of the months named above likewise differ. The Falak is such that the twelve [signs] are not equal in the sun's passage through them — the differences are as follows: in Cancer, Leo, Virgo, and Libra the sun travels thirty-one days each; in Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces the sun travels thirty days each; in Aries it travels twenty-nine days and a quarter according to the standard reckoning of thirty days; and the Falak is such that...

The beginning of the year's count starts from that time, which is why those first two are considered the beginning of Alexander the Two-Horned's reign. Caution regarding Moses, peace be upon him, in Bilays regarding adversaries; on the seventh day, the dark sheep-herding begins; on the eleventh day, the equinox is complete, and the sun enters Aries; it stays there and day and night become equal at twelve hours, and the time for bloodletting and cupping arrives.

In ancient times, according to the reckoning of the middle summer waters, the Nile would diminish at harvest time. On the third day the Arab wind called Sam blows, they say, on the fourth day Niyar-lu-la-nur comes, on the eighth day the worm Mulriji is also present, and the poisonous winds begin; on the fifteenth day Dawk completes, on the twenty-eighth day the wind called Luwajir al-Akhir comes, on the twenty-ninth day is the death of Solomon, in Tamuz.

The middle summer waters of the Nile: the Greek month Narshatyn they call it, Luwatuz-bek passes, the star Shu'ra rises in the east, on the second day Nahs, on the sixth day Makhdhur Musa is also present, on the ninth day the Sea-lou-la-nur, on the eleventh day Mir 'Attar of Balsad, on the fifteenth day the Luwadurt reaches four hours, and the sun enters Sumbula, on the twenty-first day the Sea-lou-la-nur and Makhdhur Musa are also present; the Days of Bahur are nine days in Ab.

The rising summer waters of the Nile: the Greek month called Aghustus, on the first day the flood becomes strong, Atunkel, on that first day Niyarla-Tasha begins, and Yawm al-Waqa is also in Tawakkal, which is auspicious. On the fourth day Makhdhur Musa is also in Altisundeh, the Sea-lou-la-nur, and that is the Feast of the Manifestation according to the Jews. On that same day Makhdhur Musa is present; Luwaj reaches ten hours of the day and ten hours of the night. The sun enters Virgo, and on the seventeenth and eighteenth is the Feast of the Cross.

On the eighteenth, the wind Lubariḥ Asruwan arrives, and on the nineteenth day comes salvation, the tablet is filled. On the following day the inhabitants settle. On the twenty-first there is a mixing of the two seasons and a weakening of heat — meaning the extreme heat begins to weaken. The Nile is not yet at its fullest on the twenty-fifth. On the twenty-sixth the eye-irritating wind Tahir arrives. On the twenty-eighth is the death of John. Such is the summer season, the month...

According to the Roman reckoning, it is said to be three months. After this, I will explain the autumn season. 

The Autumn Season consists of three months as mentioned. Elul (September) is the first eye of autumn. They say it has thirty days. On the first day of this month, a care must be taken. On the second day, the season of caution begins, and on the fourth day is the feast of Elijah; it is also the birthplace of Mary and Babylon, and on the same day precautions are to be observed. 

On the twenty-second (of Elul), the Nile settles, the weather becomes moderate; taking a laxative is permissible. On the twenty-fourth, the Feast of the Cross — they say one should write an amulet (talisman) on paper and hang it, and the sea becomes rough. 

The night and day become equal, and the sun reaches the equinox; on the twenty-eighth day the Seven Stars (Pleiades) rise together. On the twenty-ninth, the constellation moves westward, and from that point the gathering of cold intensifies and the stars multiply. On the twenty-first, the mind and reason become firm and settled. On the twenty-second, the sea grows rough; and on the twenty-third, the pomegranates ripen. 

Tishri al-Awwal (October) is the ninth month. They say it is called Akhtūriyūs (October). It has thirty-one days. The first day is inauspicious; the northeast wind — Saba — blows, and the third day is the Feast of Dayr al-Khalid. On the ninth day is the season of caution, and on the twelfth the sea grows rough. Toward the end of Tishri, they in their belief hold that on that day a traveler fell from the sky — that is, on the first day is the Feast of Ptarikiyah, and on that day Ishmael was brought forward for sacrifice; and on the tenth day the Companions of the Elephant (Ashab al-Fil) were destroyed near the (Sacred House). On the fourteenth day, the sun enters Scorpio, the seas become stirred, and on the fifteenth, earthquakes occur. The length of night exceeds day by three hours. The sun enters the sign of Scorpio, the seas swell. On the twenty-fifth, it is said that if one cuts trees on that day, their sap flows. And on the twenty-eighth, the Nile...

The month of Sagittarius: it is the month of caution for Moses, peace be upon him, and the birds of Egypt, but God provides abundance. In the lands of Rum (Byzantium), the cold sets in; it is the beginning of winter, and the cranes, wild geese, and large migratory birds depart according to the reckoning described. On the twenty-first day thereof, it is the day of Gog and Magog, and on that day heavy rains fall. On the twenty-fourth day, the sun reaches its utmost decline, and faces show weariness. In the lands of the earth, on the twenty-sixth and twenty-seventh days, the olive trees of Syria begin to weep sap. On the twenty-eighth day, in eight days the pressing of olives begins, and on the twenty-ninth day, the birds and the sun enter Capricorn. On the thirtieth day, which is the day of caution for Moses, and the day of the Prophet, peace be upon him, marks the beginning of fasting, a point of reckoning. Among living creatures, silence and stillness prevail; they begin to huddle together for warmth. On the twenty-fourth day of the month, drinking cold water at night is forbidden. As for the autumn season, it is reckoned by the months of Rum (Byzantine calendar), as has been mentioned. After describing those seasons, we now mention the season of Sita (winter).

Kanun al-Awwal (First Kanun / December) — This is the month of Heraklius according to the Greeks; it is called Divajerios in Greek. It has thirty-one days. On its sixth day, nine cold winds blow. On its seventh day, it is auspicious. On its eighth day, caution is advised. On its eleventh night, the cold intensifies. On its twelfth day, it is the day of the winter solstice, meaning the return of the sun — God willing, may it bring goodness.

The night is nine hours and the day is fifteen hours. The sun enters Capricorn, and such-and-such [occurs]. On the eighteenth day, it is the Day of the Death of Daniel (peace be upon him); after that, several years pass. And the congregation is forbidden from [certain things], and on the twenty-first day is the birth of Ali (peace be upon him), and twenty-nine nights pass. On the night of the twenty-ninth, the tribe of Hadinbar opens their mouths — it is said they are a tribe who suffer from moisture and coldness of the elements — in [the month of] Kanun al-Thani (December/January): The middle of the cold water [season] has arrived, and the rain and moisture and coldness of the springs [come]. In it [this time] the ancient [people] used to say that the cold has arrived and the damp settled. The fish come out of the water in it, and the colors thereof are like the sea's foam, and sixteen [days pass]. On the sixteenth day it is [the commemoration of] Musa (Moses, peace be upon him), and on the seventeenth night — it is as if [the night] of the infidels — they light fires, and on the seventeenth day it is auspicious. On the eighteenth day, the caravans depart, and within the hour a watch [guard] is set. At that hour all the fresh and salt waters become turbid — so it is reported — as if the infidels have poured something into them. In it is the Fast of the Christians, and on the nineteenth day, the sun and stars [are at such a position], and on the twentieth [the sun] enters Aquarius, and the cold intensifies. On the twenty-sixth day, Mercury enters Pisces. On the twenty-first day, the Forty Days (al-Arba'in) are complete. On the twenty-first day begins [the season of] Jajsiyan (a cold wind). On the twenty-eighth [day comes] the gathering of the secrets. [The month of] Shubat (February): This is the month of winter water. In this month, as they say in Ionia (Greek lands), [the month] is twenty-eight and a quarter days, making twenty-nine days [with the intercalary day], less a little. When thirteen [days] have passed, the air becomes like an ember — this is what they call the 'little ember.' On the ninth day it is auspicious; on the eleventh day it is [the day of] Qaws (Sagittarius), and beyond that the cold breaks from the earth and thirst [follows].

A lamp of the lily family, if lit two or three times in succession, then goes out and afterwards its remaining part fades. For a few days it continues to flicker, then after that ceases, and from this it becomes known to us that the nature of the air requires it. 'Come, O cold wind' — thus it was said among those who found themselves in it. The angels descended to the land of 'Ad telling them to depart, so that the people of 'Ad could be dealt with properly. Among the people of 'Ad there was a soothsayer woman who said that the army would return. She said to go into the desert and the angels would come. But they paid no heed to the words of that lame one, and thus they were destroyed. But — among the Arabs, before the rise of Islam, the dates [of chronology] differ.

The Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him, was sent as a prophet, and for a certain period he remained in Mecca the Ennobled, then migrated from there to Medina the Illuminated, and his Companions and the Arabs gathered there. On account of events that occurred, they began to use that event as the basis of chronology. When 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, became caliph, the senior Companions gathered before the Caliph 'Umar and said: 'It has become difficult to establish a chronology by various methods; it is necessary to choose one fixed date so that coins and official registers can be properly maintained.' 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, approved their proposal and decided that the date of the Hijra of the Messenger of God, peace be upon him, should be the foundation, and that the first year should begin with the month of Muharram. That first year's beginning fell on a Thursday — that is, the year began on a Thursday in Muharram.

[Marginal note — Section: The Fixing of the Hijri Calendar]
By the account transmitted from Abu Musa: 'Umar, may God be pleased with him, sent out saying: 'Bring me a piece of paper' — he wished to write down the date. Sufyan said: 'I will bring you a piece of paper.' The fixing of the date of the Hijra was established after consultation, and the Companions accepted it as correct and it was decreed accordingly.'

The Hijra itself is considered the starting point, specifically the fortieth day of Rabi' al-Awwal; thus the Arab months begin with Muharram and end with Dhu al-Hijja. As for the Roman calendar, the month of Tishrin al-Awwal (October) is taken as the beginning, which was established as the start of Alexander's reign, as will be explained. As for the Persian calendar, it is reckoned from the reign of a king named Yazdegerd, because it was the custom among the Persians that whenever a great king ascended the throne, the date would be reckoned from the time of his accession and named after him. When Yazdegerd ibn Shahryar ibn Khosrow came to power, they reckoned by his name, and since his reign ended during the time of Uthman ibn Affan, may God be pleased with him, the Persian calendar continued to be kept in his name. Its cycle falls on Saturdays, and it was in the eleventh year of the Hijra of the Prophet, peace be upon him, in Rabi' al-Awwal.

A solar year is the expression for the period it takes the sun to traverse all twelve of its zodiacal signs, each sign taking thirty days and some hours; thus a solar month is the period it takes the sun to traverse one zodiacal sign. A solar year is composed of solar months; the result is that each year is made up of approximately the same number of months. Because calculating the fractions became difficult, some people—namely the Persians—dropped them from consideration, calling the days of the solar year three hundred and sixty-five days, and they added the remaining days to the last month of Aban, appending them to those days. Since the Arab months have become known and some of their measures have been mentioned, let this suffice.

Sixth Section: After the months of the Persians, their detailed account follows — this section concerns the Persian months.

Since the ancient people of Persia took the celestial body (the sun) into consideration, they likewise took into account [the calculation of time], and they assigned names to the twelve months according to the solar reckoning. The names [of the months] are as follows:

• Farvardin • Ordibehesht • Khordad • Mehr • Mordad • Shahrivar • Tir • Aban • Azar • Dey
Bahman • Esfandarmaz

Each of these [months] consists of thirty days, making a total of three hundred and sixty days. And to the month of Aban five additional days are appended, which are known in that region as the 'epagomenal days' (Andargah), making the total three hundred and sixty-five days. One quarter of a day [per year] they did not count, until the astronomers [later] noted it.

When they reckoned those intercalary days at the beginning, they assigned [them] to the first month, and [the calendar] proceeded from three months onward; and the history of Jalal — that is [the calendar of] Sultan Jalal al-Dawla Malikshah the Seljuq — was named after him, and in it nine [elements] were set forth. This mention was placed at the beginning so that by it Farvardin month, the first day of which is Nowruz, would be brought to attention; and of the three months [of spring], each season consists of three months:

• Farvardin • Ordibehesht • Khordad — these three months constitute the Spring season • Mehr • Mordad • Shahrivar — these three months constitute the Autumn season • Tir • Aban • Azar — these three months constitute the Winter season
Dey • Bahman • Esfandarmaz — [these constitute the remaining season]. In the Jalali calendar and its refinement, the epagomenal days named Andargah — which Esfandarmaz Rukhshat [designates] — are distributed [accordingly], and their consideration was fixed by careful calculation and observation.

The names [of the months] in order are: 1. Farvardin 2. Ordibehesht 3. Bahman 4. Shahrivar 5. Esfandarmaz 6. Khordad 7. Mordad 8. Deyad (Dey) 9. Azar 10. Aban 11. Khur (Mehr) 12. Amah 13. Tir 14. Gush

And Malakjar — whoever gives a name to the first [day] mentioned above, designating which foods, clothing, and customs are appropriate and ordained, and whoever acts accordingly — for the days that are favorable to his heart, let him mention those affairs that concern him regarding food and drink. And whoever carries out [the fast of] Amordad for those who observe it, the food and beverage designated for it, their soul will attain joy, and from the multitude of creation, no harm shall come to those who listen to it with sincerity. It has been said: those who observe it for the sake of its lords will attain goodness and the acquisition of otherworldly felicity. So let us mention the details of Malakjar one by one, in order that the complete state of each may become known. It is Nowruz — the first day — and it is said that God Almighty sends forth on that day to all the celestial spheres what He wills.

Anecdote: It is related that 'Abd Allah ibn 'Akks, may God be pleased with him, brought a gift to the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him and his family, and it is said that there was halvah inside it, and this is the answer they gave.

The sweetness of joy: They first told of it, saying it was tremendous, and the messenger brought it. Thus those people who left their homeland were revived — some had died of plague and others from natural causes. God revealed, as stated in Surah Al-Baqarah: 'Have you not seen those who left their homes in thousands, fearing death? God said to them: Die! Then He restored them to life.' These people, it is said, were from the city of Dawur, and their story is well known; the name of that great land is Marmara — some say it is derived from the Names of God — and it is said that on the day of this gathering, 'O people of Dhann,' from morning one does not speak without a measure of gratitude as is written. And if the enemy approaches from any direction, and if the people of that place rise from sleep in the morning and make good acts of devotion — for example, if a king rises in the morning and sees his servant mounted on horseback with a falcon, and if seventy-nine warriors were gathered — these two, finding harmony, would come together for a great feast. The king would distribute among the common people gifts and rewards; and in the second category, those of his household and relatives would receive honors and gifts; and in the third category, distinguished persons would receive fine gifts and honors; and in the fourth category, his own children and descendants would receive all manner of kindness. In sum, in these five categories he would distribute gifts and honors generously to all, and after the worshippers had finished their duties.
